20151304-cbab-49e7-84b2-d3588eaa810a.content_html:
What Is Sin?

Sin is any thought or action that goes against God’s will. Christians believe sin damages the relationship between humans and God. Every time a person sins, they move further away from God. Sin can take many forms — lying, stealing, hatred, selfishness, envy and many others.

Christians believe all humans are sinful. Nobody is perfect, and everyone falls short of God’s standards. St Paul wrote: “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). This is a problem because God is holy and just — sin cannot exist in God’s presence. Humans therefore need to be saved from the consequences of their sin.

Original Sin

Original sin is the belief that all humans are born with a built-in tendency to do wrong. This idea comes from the story of Adam and Eve in Genesis 3. God placed Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden and told them not to eat from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. The serpent tempted Eve, she ate the fruit, and Adam followed.

Key Fact

Adam and Eve’s disobedience is called the Fall. Christians believe this act of disobedience broke the perfect relationship between God and humanity. As a result, all humans are born with a tendency to sin — this is original sin. It is not a specific sin a person commits, but a condition inherited from the first humans.

Catholic view: Original sin is washed away through the sacrament of baptism. This is one reason Catholics baptise infants — to free the baby from original sin as early as possible. Even after baptism, humans still have a tendency to sin (called concupiscence).

Protestant view: Most Protestants accept the concept of original sin but emphasise that salvation comes through faith in Jesus rather than through sacraments. Some Protestants do not practise infant baptism, believing a person must choose to follow Christ for themselves.

Liberal view: Some liberal Christians see the story of Adam and Eve as a myth that teaches an important truth — humans have a natural tendency to do wrong — rather than a literal historical event. The lesson is the same: humans need God’s help to overcome sin.

What Is Salvation?

Salvation means being saved from sin and its consequences — ultimately, being granted eternal life with God rather than eternal separation from God. Christians believe humans cannot save themselves because all are sinful. They need God’s help.

the specification identifies three means of salvation: law, grace and Spirit. Different Christian traditions emphasise these differently.

Salvation Through Law

Some Christians believe that following God’s laws — the Ten Commandments and the moral teachings of Jesus — is essential for salvation. By obeying God’s commands, a person shows they are devoted to God and deserving of eternal life. Catholics especially emphasise the importance of good works alongside faith — the Epistle of James states: “Faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead” (James 2:17).

Salvation Through Grace

Grace is the free, undeserved gift of God’s love. Christians believe God offers salvation not because humans deserve it, but because God loves them. Ephesians 2:8–9 states: “For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith — and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God — not by works, so that no one can boast.”

Key Fact

Protestants, especially those in the Reformed tradition, emphasise salvation by grace alone through faith alone. Humans cannot earn salvation by doing good deeds — it is a free gift from God, received through faith in Jesus Christ. Catholics believe both faith and works are necessary — grace enables good works, and both contribute to salvation.

Salvation Through the Holy Spirit

Christians believe the Holy Spirit plays an active role in salvation. The Spirit works within believers to help them recognise their sin, turn towards God, and live a holy life. Charismatic and Pentecostal Christians particularly emphasise the role of the Holy Spirit, believing it gives spiritual gifts such as speaking in tongues, prophecy and healing.

The Holy Spirit guides Christians in daily life, helping them make good decisions and resist temptation. Jesus promised: “The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things” (John 14:26). The Spirit also brings comfort in suffering, strengthens faith in difficult times, and empowers Christians to share the gospel with others.

The Role of Christ in Salvation

All Christians agree that Jesus Christ is central to salvation. Without Jesus, humans would remain trapped in sin with no way back to God. Jesus’s death and resurrection made salvation possible.

Atonement

Atonement literally means “at-one-ment” — making God and humanity “at one” again. It is the belief that Jesus’s death on the cross restored the broken relationship between God and humans caused by sin. Through his sacrifice, Jesus took the punishment that humans deserved.

Key Fact

Isaiah 53:5 prophesied the atonement: “He was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.” Christians believe this prophecy was fulfilled by Jesus on the cross.

Substitutionary atonement: Jesus took the place of sinful humans and bore the punishment they deserved. He was a substitute — dying instead of humanity. This view is common among evangelical Protestants.

Satisfaction theory: Human sin offended God’s honour and justice. Only a perfect sacrifice could satisfy God’s justice. Jesus, being sinless, was the only one who could offer this perfect payment. This view is associated with Anselm of Canterbury and is common in Catholic theology.

Moral example: Some liberal Christians see Jesus’s death less as a payment for sin and more as a supreme example of self-sacrificing love. His willingness to die inspires Christians to live selflessly and sacrificially for others.

Regardless of which understanding they hold, all Christians agree that the atonement makes salvation available. Jesus’s sacrifice opened the door for humans to be reconciled with God, forgiven for their sins, and given the promise of eternal life.

2cb81065-b9c3-43e8-9b90-d4322738dbe3.title: Festivals and Commemorations
2cb81065-b9c3-43e8-9b90-d4322738dbe3.content_html:
Festivals and Commemorations in Islam

Muslims celebrate several important festivals throughout the year. You need to know three: Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, and Ashura. Each festival has distinct origins, and Muslims celebrate them in different ways depending on their denomination.

Eid al-Fitr — The Festival of Breaking the Fast

Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, the holy month of fasting. The word “Eid” means “festival” and “Fitr” means “breaking the fast.” It is a joyful celebration that thanks Allah for the strength to complete the fast and for the revelation of the Qur’an, which took place during Ramadan.

Key Fact

The Qur’an states: “He wants that you must complete the same number of days, and that you must magnify Allah for having guided you so that you may be grateful to Him” (2:185). This verse connects the completion of Ramadan fasting directly to the celebration of Eid al-Fitr.

Preparations begin before the day itself. Muslims send cards, decorate their homes, buy new clothes, and prepare special food and gifts. On the morning of Eid, Muslims rise early, bathe, and eat something sweet — traditionally dates — before attending the Eid prayer. The Prophet Muhammad himself consumed dates before the Eid prayer, and Muslims follow this Sunnah.

Before the Eid prayer, Muslims give Zakat al-Fitr — a small charitable donation (approximately £2–£5) so that poorer Muslims can also celebrate. The Eid prayer takes place at the mosque or in an open area such as a park. After the prayer, the Imam delivers a sermon. Muslims then exchange gifts, visit friends and family, and share a special meal together. It is also Sunnah to take a different route home from the one taken to the prayer. Many Muslims visit the cemetery to remember loved ones and forgive friends or relatives they have fallen out with.

In Muslim-majority countries, Eid al-Fitr is a public holiday. In the UK, British Muslims are often allowed a day off school or work. The festival reinforces the sense of ummah (community) as Muslims come together to celebrate after a month of shared spiritual discipline.

Eid al-Adha — The Festival of Sacrifice

Eid al-Adha takes place during the month of Dhul Hijjah and coincides with the annual Hajj pilgrimage. It commemorates the Prophet Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son when commanded by Allah. According to Islamic tradition, Ibrahim told his son of Allah’s command, and his son replied that they must do as Allah demanded. However, at the moment of sacrifice, Allah provided a ram to be killed instead. This demonstrated Ibrahim’s complete submission to the will of Allah.

Key Fact

The Qur’an teaches that Ibrahim agreed to sacrifice his son even though he was tempted by Shaytan (the devil). At three places, the angel Jibril told Ibrahim to “Pelt him,” so Ibrahim threw seven pebbles and Shaytan left. This event is re-enacted during Hajj at the Jamarat stone pillars.

The central act of Eid al-Adha is the Qurbani — the sacrifice of an animal, usually a sheep or goat. The meat is divided into three portions: one third for the family, one third for friends and neighbours, and one third distributed to the poor. This ensures that everyone, regardless of wealth, can share in the celebration.

Muslims also attend special Eid prayers at the mosque, listen to a sermon, wear their best clothes, and exchange gifts. For pilgrims on Hajj, this is a particularly solemn moment — men shave their heads and women cut a lock of hair, symbolising the end of the main pilgrimage rituals. The festival lasts for up to three days.

Ashura — A Day of Remembrance

Ashura falls on the 10th day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar. It is significant for both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims, but its origins and the way it is commemorated differ greatly between the two denominations. This makes Ashura one of the clearest examples of Sunni–Shi’a differences in practice.

Key Fact

For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura commemorates the martyrdom of Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. For Sunni Muslims, it recalls the day Allah saved Musa (Moses) and the Israelites from slavery in Egypt by parting the Red Sea.

After the death of the Prophet Muhammad, a dispute arose over who should lead the Muslim community. Shi’a Muslims believed leadership should stay within the Prophet’s family. In 680 CE, Yazid succeeded his father Muawiyah as Caliph. Yazid demanded that Husayn, Muhammad’s grandson and son of Imam Ali, pledge allegiance to him. Husayn refused because he believed Yazid was religiously misguided and that the agreement for leadership to remain within the Prophet’s family had been broken.

The people of Kufa invited Husayn to join them in opposition to Yazid. On his way to Kufa, Yazid’s army forced Husayn, his family, and a small group of supporters to stop at Karbala. They were denied water and food. After about seven days, Husayn and most of his family and companions were killed in battle. Husayn was beheaded. Shi’a Muslims regard Husayn and his followers as martyrs who chose death rather than compromise their beliefs.

Shi’a Muslims treat Ashura as an intense day of mourning and sorrow. Many wear black mourning clothes, participate in processions to mark the martyrdom, and listen to accounts and poems about Husayn’s death, which may lead to weeping. Some Shi’a Muslims make pilgrimage to Husayn’s shrine in Karbala (called Mashad al-Husayn). Some practise self-flagellation or give blood to remember the blood shed by the martyrs. Others pray and visit the mosque, reflecting on how a true Muslim should be steadfast in their faith as Husayn was.

Sunni Muslims commemorate Ashura primarily through voluntary fasting, following the example of the Prophet Muhammad, who fasted when he learned that the Jews of Medina fasted on this day to remember Allah saving Musa from the Egyptians. Sunni Muslims may also help the less fortunate, repent their sins, ask for forgiveness, and pray at the mosque. In Turkey, some eat a special pudding called Nuh’s pudding.

Ashura is sometimes debated as a term. Some argue it should not be called a “festival” or “celebration” at all, particularly for Shi’a Muslims, because the mood is one of grief and mourning rather than joy. This contrasts sharply with the celebratory atmosphere of Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha. Nevertheless, it remains one of the most significant dates in the Islamic calendar.

5cd591ad-b5bb-4adb-ac6f-eaf60f0d1271.title: Jihad
5cd591ad-b5bb-4adb-ac6f-eaf60f0d1271.content_html:
Jihad — Striving in the Way of God

The word jihad is one of the most misunderstood terms in Islam. It simply means “struggle” or “striving” and refers to the effort every Muslim must make to follow God’s path. Islam distinguishes between two forms of jihad: greater jihad and lesser jihad.

Greater Jihad — The Inner Struggle

Greater jihad is the daily personal battle every Muslim faces to live according to Allah’s will. It includes resisting temptation, overcoming selfishness, being honest, showing compassion, and striving to become a better person. The Prophet Muhammad is reported to have told soldiers returning from battle: “You have come from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the struggle of a person against their own desires” (Hadith).

Key Fact

Greater jihad is considered more important than lesser jihad because it is a lifelong, continuous struggle. It includes studying the Qur’an, performing the Five Pillars, treating others justly, resisting greed and selfishness, and striving to improve oneself spiritually. Every Muslim engages in greater jihad every day.

Lesser Jihad — The Physical Struggle

Lesser jihad refers to the physical or military struggle to defend Islam when it is under threat. It is permitted only as a last resort and is subject to strict conditions. The Qur’an states: “Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits” (Qur’an 2:190). This verse makes clear that aggression and excess are forbidden.

Islamic teaching sets strict conditions that must be met before lesser jihad can be declared:

It must be defensive: Lesser jihad is only permitted to protect Islam, Muslim lands or oppressed people from attack. Aggressive warfare for conquest, territory or personal gain is forbidden.

It must be a last resort: All peaceful means of resolving the conflict — negotiation, diplomacy, treaties — must be exhausted first.

It must be declared by a recognised religious authority: No individual or group can declare jihad on their own. It requires the authority of a legitimate Muslim leader or scholar.

It must be proportionate: The Qur’an forbids excess (“do not overstep the limits” — 2:190). Civilians, women, children, the elderly, crops and livestock must not be targeted. Prisoners must be treated humanely.

It must stop when the enemy seeks peace: “If they incline towards peace, you must incline towards it too” (Qur’an 8:61).

Key Fact

Lesser jihad is only permitted when it is defensive, a last resort, declared by a legitimate authority, proportionate, and must cease when the enemy seeks peace. The Qur’an explicitly forbids aggression: “Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits” (2:190).

Both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims recognise greater and lesser jihad. However, jihad holds a particularly prominent place in Shi’a Islam as one of the Ten Obligatory Acts. Some Shi’a scholars have historically taught that only a divinely appointed Imam has the authority to declare lesser jihad, which in practice means it cannot be declared while the twelfth Imam remains in occultation. This view restricts the circumstances under which lesser jihad can occur. Other Shi’a scholars argue that senior religious leaders may authorise defensive action in the Imam’s absence.

Islamic Festivals and Commemorations

Festivals play an important role in Muslim life, bringing communities together in celebration and remembrance. The specification requires knowledge of three: Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr, and Ashura.

Id-ul-Adha — The Festival of Sacrifice

Id-ul-Adha falls during the month of Dhul Hijjah and coincides with the Hajj pilgrimage. It commemorates the moment when Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his son in obedience to God’s command. At the last moment, God provided a ram to sacrifice instead, showing that Ibrahim had passed the ultimate test of faith. Muslims around the world — not just those on Hajj — celebrate by sacrificing an animal (usually a sheep, goat or cow). The meat is divided into three portions: one for the family, one for friends and neighbours, and one for the poor.

Id-ul-Fitr — The Festival of Breaking the Fast

Id-ul-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. After a month of fasting, prayer and self-reflection, Muslims celebrate with special prayers at the mosque, new clothes, festive meals, gifts and visiting family and friends. Before the Eid prayer, Muslims pay Zakat-ul-Fitr — a small charitable donation to ensure that even the poorest members of the community can join in the celebration. It is a day of gratitude to Allah for the strength to complete the fast and a time of joy shared with the whole community.

Ashura falls on the 10th day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar. Its meaning differs greatly between Sunni and Shi’a Muslims.

For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is a day of voluntary fasting. It commemorates the day when God saved the Prophet Musa (Moses) and the Israelites from the Pharaoh by parting the Red Sea. Muhammad fasted on this day and encouraged his followers to do the same.

For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year. It commemorates the martyrdom of Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, who was killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Husayn had refused to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad Caliph Yazid, whom Shi’a Muslims considered unjust and illegitimate. His death is seen as the ultimate sacrifice for justice and truth. Shi’a Muslims observe Ashura with mourning processions, dramatic re-enactments of the Battle of Karbala, and expressions of grief. It is a day of deep sorrow, not celebration.

Key Fact

Ashura shows the sharpest divide between Sunni and Shi’a practice. Sunni Muslims observe it as a day of fasting linked to Musa (Moses). Shi’a Muslims observe it as a day of intense mourning for Husayn’s martyrdom at Karbala in 680 CE — one of the most significant events in Shi’a history.

61e454f6-9505-467e-b3b5-6142f300954f.title: The Covenant: Abraham, Moses and the Promised Land
61e454f6-9505-467e-b3b5-6142f300954f.content_html:
What Is a Covenant?

A covenant is not a simple contract. It is a solemn, binding relationship — in the Jewish context, an agreement between God and the Jewish people that carries profound obligations and promises on both sides. The covenants at the heart of Jewish theology are not merely ancient historical events; Jewish teaching holds that they remain active and binding today. They define who the Jewish people are in relation to God and what God expects of them.

Two covenants stand at the foundation of Jewish belief: the covenant with Abraham (recorded in Genesis 12 and 17) and the covenant at Sinai (recorded in Exodus 20), sealed through the giving of the Torah and the Ten Commandments.

The Covenant With Abraham

In Genesis 12:1-3, God calls Abraham to leave his homeland and travel to a land that God will show him. The promise is threefold: land (“the promised land”), descendants (a great nation), and blessing (through Abraham’s descendants, all the families of the earth will be blessed). This is one of the most important passages in the Tenakh because it establishes the special relationship between God and the Jewish people and holds out a universal vision — Abraham’s family becoming a source of blessing for the entire world.

The covenant with Abraham was renewed and developed in Genesis 17, where God gives Abraham the sign of Brit Milah (circumcision) as the physical mark of the covenant. Every Jewish male circumcised at eight days old carries the sign of this covenant in his body — making it an embodied, communal identity marker across all generations.

Key Fact

The Covenant with Abraham (Genesis 12:1-3) contains three promises: a land (Canaan, the “promised land”); descendants (a great nation); and blessing to all peoples of the earth through Abraham’s family. These promises form the bedrock of Jewish identity and hope.

Moses and the Covenant at Sinai

Moses is the most significant human figure in the Torah. After leading the Israelites out of slavery in Egypt, Moses ascended Mount Sinai and received God’s revelation. The covenant made at Sinai is qualitatively different from the covenant with Abraham: at Sinai, the entire Israelite people — not just one individual and his family — entered into a binding agreement with God. They would be God’s people; God would be their God. In return, they accepted the Torah and its commandments as their way of life.

The significance of Moses cannot be overstated. He is described in the Torah as the greatest of all prophets — the only person who spoke with God “face to face, as a man speaks to his friend” (Deuteronomy 34:10). Jewish teaching holds that no prophet would arise in Israel greater than Moses, and his role as the transmitter of the Torah — both written and oral — makes him the founding teacher of the Jewish tradition.

The Ten Commandments

The Ten Commandments (Decalogue) recorded in Exodus 20:1-17 are the most prominent and widely recognised part of the Sinai revelation. They divide into two groups: the first four concern the relationship between humanity and God (no other gods; no idols; not taking God’s name in vain; keeping Shabbat holy), and the remaining six concern the relationship between people (honour your parents; do not murder; do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not give false witness; do not covet).

Jewish tradition teaches that the full covenant at Sinai involved not just the Ten Commandments but the complete Torah — 613 commandments covering every aspect of life. The Ten Commandments are understood as a summary or foundational statement rather than the entirety of divine law. In synagogue services, the Ten Commandments are recited on certain occasions, and many synagogues display them on plaques near the ark.

The Torah divides the 613 mitzvot into two broad categories. Mitzvot between man and God (bein adam l’Makom) include prayer, observing Shabbat and festivals, keeping dietary laws, and daily rituals of study and gratitude. These sanctify the individual’s relationship with the divine. Mitzvot between man and man (bein adam l’chavero) include not stealing, not lying, caring for the poor, and treating every person with dignity. These sanctify communal life. Jewish teaching holds that, for the mitzvot between man and man, God’s forgiveness on Yom Kippur cannot substitute for making direct amends to the person wronged.

The “promised land” (Eretz Yisrael) has remained a central element in Jewish consciousness throughout history, even during centuries of exile. Orthodox communities typically understand the promise of the land as literal and ongoing. Some Orthodox Jews make aliyah (immigration to Israel) as a religious act, fulfilling the covenant. Reform and Liberal communities hold more varied views: many affirm a spiritual or cultural connection to the land of Israel without prioritising physical settlement as a religious obligation. It is important to note that these are internal Jewish theological debates — the exam expects you to describe what different Jewish traditions teach, not to adjudicate the political dimensions.

Key Fact

Two foundational covenants: (1) Abraham — Genesis 12:1-3: land, descendants, blessing for all peoples. Sign: Brit Milah (circumcision). (2) Sinai — Exodus 20:1-17: the entire Israelite people accept God’s Torah and commandments; God becomes their God. Moses is the mediator. Together these covenants define Jewish identity and obligation.

63c10787-aeda-40ef-8709-bfb569454ec9.title: Mission, Evangelism and World Poverty
63c10787-aeda-40ef-8709-bfb569454ec9.content_html:
The Place of Mission and Evangelism

Mission is at the heart of Christianity. Christians believe they have a duty to share the good news about Jesus Christ with non-believers. This calling comes directly from the words of Jesus himself. Evangelism is one of the main ways this mission is carried out — through public preaching, personal conversations, and organised events that invite people to learn about the Christian faith.

Key Fact

Mission means “sent out” — it refers to the duty of Christians to go into the world and spread their faith. Evangelism is the practice of spreading the Christian gospel by public preaching or personal witness.

The Great Commission

The Great Commission is the instruction Jesus gave to his disciples after his resurrection. It is recorded in Matthew 28:16–20. Jesus told his eleven disciples: “Go, then, to all peoples everywhere and make them my disciples: baptise them in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and teach them to obey everything I have commanded you.”

This passage is significant for three reasons. First, Jesus commands his followers to make disciples of all nations — not just believers, but people who actively follow his teachings. Second, he instructs them to baptise new converts, showing that baptism has been central to the Church from the very beginning. Third, he tells them to teach obedience to his commandments, meaning the disciples must pass on Jesus’ moral and spiritual teachings.

Jesus also said: “Come, follow me… and I will send you out to fish for people” (Matthew 4:19). At Pentecost, the Holy Spirit gave the disciples the gifts and courage they needed to carry out this mission.

Christians spread their faith in several ways. They talk to friends, family, and colleagues about their beliefs. Some become missionaries, travelling to other countries to preach and carry out humanitarian work among the poor and disadvantaged. Others use social media, television channels like God TV, and Christian radio to reach wider audiences. Many churches invite people to attend events, services, or informal gatherings as a first step towards faith.

Church Growth

The Church is growing rapidly in South America, Africa, and Asia, though growth has slowed in the USA, Europe, and the Middle East. Worldwide, around 80,000 people become Christians each day, and over 500 new churches begin. The Church’s mission is to make new disciples, not just new believers — this means evangelism should be followed by training new converts in the way of following Jesus and spreading the faith.

The Alpha Course — started as a way to help church members understand the basics of the Christian faith. It is now used as an introduction for anyone interested in learning about Christianity. Described as “an opportunity to explore the meaning of life,” Alpha courses are held in homes, workplaces, universities, prisons, and churches.

The Church Army — helps people find faith and works with vulnerable and marginalised people in society, bringing them into the Church.

Christ for all Nations (CfaN) — an international evangelism organisation that holds large-scale events to spread the Christian gospel worldwide.

Fresh Expressions of Church — new and creative forms of church designed to engage with people who might not otherwise think of attending a traditional church service.

The Church’s Response to World Poverty

Christians believe they have a responsibility to help those living in poverty because Jesus taught that this was important. The causes of world poverty include debt, natural disasters, disease, conflict, unfair trade, lack of education, inadequate healthcare, and corrupt leaders. Three major Christian charities work to address these causes.

Key Fact

Three key Christian charities that respond to world poverty are CAFOD, Tearfund, and Christian Aid. Each provides both emergency relief and long-term development support, motivated by Jesus’ teachings about caring for the poor.

CAFOD (Catholic Agency for Overseas Development) works to train and support communities to work their way out of poverty. It provides short-term aid such as food, water, and shelter during disasters. CAFOD also campaigns with the government and encourages Catholic churches and schools to donate money and pray for those in need.

Tearfund works with churches worldwide to lift people out of poverty. It supplies emergency aid after natural disasters and provides long-term aid to help communities become more self-reliant. Tearfund is supported by fundraising and prayer from churches.

Christian Aid supports projects to encourage sustainable development. It provides emergency relief such as food, water, shelter, and sanitation. Christian Aid also campaigns to end poverty and global warming, and works to encourage fair trade.

Biblical Teachings on Poverty

Jesus’ teachings provide the motivation for Christian responses to world poverty. Jesus once told a rich man to sell everything and give to the poor, saying: “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for someone who is rich to enter the Kingdom of God.” The Parable of the Rich Man and Lazarus tells of a wealthy man who ends up in hell for ignoring a beggar at his gate.

The Bible also teaches: “Faith without action is dead” (James 2:26), meaning Christians must put their beliefs into practical action. In 1 John 3:17–18, it says: “If anyone has material possessions and sees a brother or sister in need but has no pity on them, how can the love of God be in that person? Dear children, let us not love with words or speech but with actions and truth.”

Key Fact

The Parable of the Sheep and Goats (Matthew 25) teaches that those who help the hungry, thirsty, and needy are serving God himself: “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me.”

726365d6-d634-483d-9ea8-7e026607d441.title: Tawhid, the Nature of Allah & Angels
726365d6-d634-483d-9ea8-7e026607d441.content_html:
Tawhid — The Oneness of God

Tawhid is the single most important belief in Islam. It means the absolute oneness of Allah — there is no God but Allah, and nothing can be compared to Him. Tawhid is the foundation of everything a Muslim believes and does. It is the first part of the Shahadah (declaration of faith): “There is no God but Allah.”

Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) is the key Qur’anic text on Tawhid. It declares: “He is Allah, the One. Allah is Eternal and Absolute. None is born of Him, He is unborn. There is none like unto Him.” This short surah makes clear that Allah is unique, has always existed, was never created and cannot be compared to anything in creation.

Key Fact

Surah 112:1–4 is essential for the exam. It states that Allah is One, Eternal and Absolute, was not born and did not give birth, and nothing is comparable to Him. This surah is recited daily by Muslims and summarises the entire concept of Tawhid.

The opposite of Tawhid is Shirk — associating partners with Allah or giving God-like qualities to anything else. Shirk is considered the worst sin in Islam and the only sin Allah will not forgive. This is why Muslims do not create images of Allah or Muhammad, and why Islamic art uses geometric patterns and calligraphy rather than depictions of God.

The Nature and Qualities of Allah

Muslims believe Allah has many qualities, described throughout the Qur’an. You need to know five key attributes:

Omnipotence (Al-Qadir): Allah is all-powerful. He created the universe from nothing and sustains all life. Nothing is beyond His ability. Surah 2:20 states: “Allah has power over everything.”

Beneficence (Ar-Rahman): Allah is all-good and provides for His creation. Every surah of the Qur’an except one opens with: “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.” Allah provides food, water, shelter and guidance for all people.

Mercy (Ar-Rahim): Allah is the Most Merciful. He forgives those who sincerely repent. Surah 39:53 says: “Do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.” Muslims believe Allah’s mercy outweighs His wrath.

Fairness and Justice (Al-Adl): Allah treats all people fairly and never acts unjustly. Every person will be judged equally on the Day of Judgement. This quality is especially emphasised in Shi’a Islam as Adalat, one of the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din.

Justice (Adalat in Shi’a Islam): While both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims agree that Allah is just, Shi’a Islam elevates this quality to one of its core beliefs. Surah 16:90 states: “Indeed Allah commands you towards justice.” This means Allah will hold everyone accountable and will never punish the innocent.

Immanence and Transcendence

The spec asks about two contrasting ideas regarding Allah’s relationship with the world:

Transcendence means Allah is beyond and above creation. He exists outside of time, space and the physical world. Muslims emphasise that Allah is utterly different from anything humans can imagine — this is why Surah 112 says “There is none like unto Him.” Allah cannot be fully understood by the human mind.

Immanence means Allah is present and involved in the world. Despite being beyond creation, Allah is closer to every person than their own jugular vein (Surah 50:16). He hears prayers, guides individuals and intervenes in the world. Muslims experience Allah’s immanence through prayer, the Qur’an and the natural world.

Key Fact

Muslims believe Allah is both transcendent (above and beyond creation) and immanent (close and involved in the world). These ideas are not contradictory — Allah is so powerful that He can be beyond the universe and yet closer to a person than their own jugular vein (Surah 50:16).

Angels (Malaikah)

Belief in angels is the second article of Sunni faith. Malaikah are beings created by Allah from divine light (Nur). Unlike humans, angels have no free will — they obey Allah’s commands without question. Surah 35:1 describes them as “messengers with two, three, four pairs of wings.”

Jibril (Gabriel) is the most important angel. He delivered the Qur’an to the Prophet Muhammad over a period of 23 years, beginning in 610 CE during the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr). Without Jibril, Muhammad would not have received Allah’s revelation, and the Qur’an would not exist. Jibril also appeared to Ibrahim and Maryam (Mary), making him the chief messenger between Allah and humanity.

Mika’il (Michael) is the angel of mercy and provision. He is responsible for providing nourishment to human bodies and souls, and controls the natural world — rain, weather and harvest. Muslims believe Mika’il distributes Allah’s blessings throughout creation.

Angels perform several roles: they deliver revelations from Allah to prophets, they record every person’s good and bad deeds (the recording angels sit on each shoulder), they welcome the righteous into paradise, and they will be present at the Day of Judgement. The angel Israfil will blow the trumpet to announce the Day of Judgement, and Azra’il (the Angel of Death) takes souls at the moment of death.

Belief in angels influences Muslims today because it reminds them that their actions are always being recorded. This encourages moral behaviour, honesty and mindfulness in daily life. If a Muslim is tempted to do wrong, the knowledge that an angel is recording the deed acts as a powerful deterrent.

Angels are central to Islam because they connect Allah to humanity. Without Jibril, the Qur’an would not have been revealed. Without the recording angels, there would be no account of human deeds for the Day of Judgement. Belief in Malaikah therefore reinforces belief in the Qur’an, prophethood and the afterlife — linking multiple articles of faith together.

7d0b4040-9861-4ff3-a6dc-8392165db0b8.title: Angels and Predestination
7d0b4040-9861-4ff3-a6dc-8392165db0b8.content_html:
Risalah — Prophethood

Risalah means prophethood. Muslims believe Allah did not leave humanity without guidance — He sent prophets (messengers) at different times throughout history to teach people how to live according to His will. Prophets are human beings chosen by Allah. They are not divine, but they are considered sinless (ma’sum) and perfectly obedient to God.

The Qur’an mentions 25 prophets by name, but Muslims believe there were many more — some traditions say 124,000. Every nation received at least one prophet. The specification requires knowledge of three key prophets: Adam, Ibrahim (Abraham) and Muhammad.

Adam was the first human and the first prophet. Allah created Adam from clay and breathed life into him. Adam was placed in the Garden of Eden with Hawwa (Eve). When they disobeyed Allah by eating from the forbidden tree, they were sent to earth. However, Adam repented sincerely and Allah forgave him. In Islam, Adam is not seen as carrying “original sin” — his repentance was accepted, and every person is born sinless.

Ibrahim (Abraham) is one of the most important prophets in Islam, known as “Khalilullah” — the Friend of Allah. Ibrahim demonstrated perfect submission to God. When Allah commanded him to sacrifice his son Isma’il, Ibrahim was willing to obey, proving his total faith. Allah intervened and provided a ram instead. This event is commemorated during the festival of Id-ul-Adha. Ibrahim also rebuilt the Ka’aba in Makkah with Isma’il, establishing the site of Hajj.

Muhammad is the final and most important prophet — the “Seal of the Prophets” (Khatam an-Nabiyyin). Surah 33:40 states: “Muhammad is… the messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets.” This means no more prophets will come after him. Muhammad received the Qur’an from the angel Jibril over 23 years, beginning in 610 CE. His life and teachings (the Hadith) are a model for all Muslims to follow. Muhammad’s example is known as the Sunnah.

Key Fact

Muhammad is called the “Seal of the Prophets” (Surah 33:40), meaning he is the last and final messenger of Allah. No new prophets will come after him. His message — the Qur’an — is considered the complete and final revelation from God.

The Holy Books (Kutub)

Muslims believe Allah revealed His guidance through several holy books, each given to a different prophet. Belief in these books is the third article of Sunni faith (Kutub). However, Muslims believe that all previous scriptures were either lost, altered or corrupted over time. Only the Qur’an remains in its original, unchanged form.

The Qur’an was revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril over 23 years. It contains 114 surahs (chapters) and is considered the literal, unchanged word of Allah in Arabic. It is the supreme authority in Islam — every other source of guidance is secondary to it. Muslims treat the physical Qur’an with great respect: it is kept on the highest shelf, hands are washed before reading it, and nothing is placed on top of it.

The Torah (Tawrat) was revealed to the Prophet Musa (Moses). It contained Allah’s laws and guidance for the Israelites.

The Psalms (Zabur) were revealed to the Prophet Dawud (David). They contained hymns and praises to Allah.

The Gospel (Injil) was revealed to the Prophet Isa (Jesus). It contained guidance and teachings from Allah for the people of that time.

The Scrolls of Abraham (Suhuf Ibrahim) were among the earliest revelations, given to the Prophet Ibrahim. They have been lost entirely.

Key Fact

The Qur’an has supreme authority in Islam because Muslims believe it is the only holy book that has never been changed or corrupted. It is the direct word of Allah, revealed in Arabic through Jibril, and it supersedes all previous scriptures.

The Qur’an: Revelation and Authority

The Qur’an was revealed to Muhammad beginning on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) in approximately 610 CE. Muhammad was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira near Makkah when the angel Jibril appeared and commanded him to “Read!” (Surah 96:1–5). Muhammad could not read, but the words were pressed into his heart. Revelations continued for the next 23 years until Muhammad’s death in 632 CE.

The Qur’an’s authority in Islam is absolute. It is the primary source of Shari’ah (Islamic law) and provides guidance on worship, morality, family life, justice and social conduct. When a question arises, Muslims turn first to the Qur’an, then to the Hadith and Sunnah, and then to scholarly interpretation.

The Imamate in Shi’a Islam

The Imamate is the fourth root of Usul ad-Din and is unique to Shi’a Islam. Shi’a Muslims believe that after Muhammad’s death, leadership of the Muslim community should have passed to his cousin and son-in-law Ali, and then through a line of twelve Imams descended from Muhammad’s family (Ahl al-Bayt).

Divine appointment: Shi’a Muslims believe each Imam was chosen by Allah, not elected by the community. This gives them a religious authority that Sunni caliphs did not claim.

Infallibility: The Imams are considered ma’sum (sinless and infallible). They cannot make mistakes in matters of faith and are perfect interpreters of the Qur’an and Islamic law.

The Twelfth Imam: Shi’a Muslims believe the twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, went into “occultation” (hiding) in 874 CE. He is believed to be alive and will return at the end of time as a messianic figure to establish justice and peace on earth.

Influence today: Because the twelfth Imam is in hiding, Shi’a scholars (ayatollahs and mujtahids) act as his representatives, interpreting Islamic law on his behalf. This gives senior Shi’a clergy a level of religious authority that has no parallel in Sunni Islam.

The Imamate is a key difference between Sunni and Shi’a Islam. Sunni Muslims do not believe in divinely appointed, infallible leaders after Muhammad. They followed elected caliphs and rely on scholarly consensus for interpretation of Islamic law. For Shi’a Muslims, the Imamate is not merely a political institution — it is a core theological belief about how Allah continues to guide humanity.

92a581f4-9585-4df5-8190-332ddace0a47.title: Jihad & Islamic Festivals
92a581f4-9585-4df5-8190-332ddace0a47.content_html:
Jihad — Striving in the Way of God

The word jihad is one of the most misunderstood terms in Islam. It simply means “struggle” or “striving” and refers to the effort every Muslim must make to follow God’s path. Islam distinguishes between two forms of jihad: greater jihad and lesser jihad.

Greater Jihad — The Inner Struggle

Greater jihad is the daily personal battle every Muslim faces to live according to Allah’s will. It includes resisting temptation, overcoming selfishness, being honest, showing compassion, and striving to become a better person. The Prophet Muhammad is reported to have told soldiers returning from battle: “You have come from the lesser jihad to the greater jihad — the struggle of a person against their own desires” (Hadith).

Key Fact

Greater jihad is considered more important than lesser jihad because it is a lifelong, continuous struggle. It includes studying the Qur’an, performing the Five Pillars, treating others justly, resisting greed and selfishness, and striving to improve oneself spiritually. Every Muslim engages in greater jihad every day.

Lesser Jihad — The Physical Struggle

Lesser jihad refers to the physical or military struggle to defend Islam when it is under threat. It is permitted only as a last resort and is subject to strict conditions. The Qur’an states: “Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits” (Qur’an 2:190). This verse makes clear that aggression and excess are forbidden.

Islamic teaching sets strict conditions that must be met before lesser jihad can be declared:

It must be defensive: Lesser jihad is only permitted to protect Islam, Muslim lands or oppressed people from attack. Aggressive warfare for conquest, territory or personal gain is forbidden.

It must be a last resort: All peaceful means of resolving the conflict — negotiation, diplomacy, treaties — must be exhausted first.

It must be declared by a recognised religious authority: No individual or group can declare jihad on their own. It requires the authority of a legitimate Muslim leader or scholar.

It must be proportionate: The Qur’an forbids excess (“do not overstep the limits” — 2:190). Civilians, women, children, the elderly, crops and livestock must not be targeted. Prisoners must be treated humanely.

It must stop when the enemy seeks peace: “If they incline towards peace, you must incline towards it too” (Qur’an 8:61).

Key Fact

Lesser jihad is only permitted when it is defensive, a last resort, declared by a legitimate authority, proportionate, and must cease when the enemy seeks peace. The Qur’an explicitly forbids aggression: “Fight in God’s cause against those who fight you, but do not overstep the limits” (2:190).

Both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims recognise greater and lesser jihad. However, jihad holds a particularly prominent place in Shi’a Islam as one of the Ten Obligatory Acts. Some Shi’a scholars have historically taught that only a divinely appointed Imam has the authority to declare lesser jihad, which in practice means it cannot be declared while the twelfth Imam remains in occultation. This view restricts the circumstances under which lesser jihad can occur. Other Shi’a scholars argue that senior religious leaders may authorise defensive action in the Imam’s absence.

Islamic Festivals and Commemorations

Festivals play an important role in Muslim life, bringing communities together in celebration and remembrance. The specification requires knowledge of three: Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr, and Ashura.

Id-ul-Adha — The Festival of Sacrifice

Id-ul-Adha falls during the month of Dhul Hijjah and coincides with the Hajj pilgrimage. It commemorates the moment when Ibrahim was willing to sacrifice his son in obedience to God’s command. At the last moment, God provided a ram to sacrifice instead, showing that Ibrahim had passed the ultimate test of faith. Muslims around the world — not just those on Hajj — celebrate by sacrificing an animal (usually a sheep, goat or cow). The meat is divided into three portions: one for the family, one for friends and neighbours, and one for the poor.

Id-ul-Fitr — The Festival of Breaking the Fast

Id-ul-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. After a month of fasting, prayer and self-reflection, Muslims celebrate with special prayers at the mosque, new clothes, festive meals, gifts and visiting family and friends. Before the Eid prayer, Muslims pay Zakat-ul-Fitr — a small charitable donation to ensure that even the poorest members of the community can join in the celebration. It is a day of gratitude to Allah for the strength to complete the fast and a time of joy shared with the whole community.

Ashura falls on the 10th day of Muharram, the first month of the Islamic calendar. Its meaning differs greatly between Sunni and Shi’a Muslims.

For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is a day of voluntary fasting. It commemorates the day when God saved the Prophet Musa (Moses) and the Israelites from the Pharaoh by parting the Red Sea. Muhammad fasted on this day and encouraged his followers to do the same.

For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year. It commemorates the martyrdom of Husayn, the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, who was killed at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Husayn had refused to pledge allegiance to the Umayyad Caliph Yazid, whom Shi’a Muslims considered unjust and illegitimate. His death is seen as the ultimate sacrifice for justice and truth. Shi’a Muslims observe Ashura with mourning processions, dramatic re-enactments of the Battle of Karbala, and expressions of grief. It is a day of deep sorrow, not celebration.

Key Fact

Ashura shows the sharpest divide between Sunni and Shi’a practice. Sunni Muslims observe it as a day of fasting linked to Musa (Moses). Shi’a Muslims observe it as a day of intense mourning for Husayn’s martyrdom at Karbala in 680 CE — one of the most significant events in Shi’a history.

95bb2c11-feec-4a6c-a2d9-f1b604f0fd31.title: Sin, Salvation & Atonement
95bb2c11-feec-4a6c-a2d9-f1b604f0fd31.content_html:
What Is Sin?

Sin is any thought or action that goes against God’s will. Christians believe sin damages the relationship between humans and God. Every time a person sins, they move further away from God. Sin can take many forms — lying, stealing, hatred, selfishness, envy and many others.

Christians believe all humans are sinful. Nobody is perfect, and everyone falls short of God’s standards. St Paul wrote: “For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). This is a problem because God is holy and just — sin cannot exist in God’s presence. Humans therefore need to be saved from the consequences of their sin.

Original Sin

Original sin is the belief that all humans are born with a built-in tendency to do wrong. This idea comes from the story of Adam and Eve in Genesis 3. God placed Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden and told them not to eat from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. The serpent tempted Eve, she ate the fruit, and Adam followed.

Key Fact

Adam and Eve’s disobedience is called the Fall. Christians believe this act of disobedience broke the perfect relationship between God and humanity. As a result, all humans are born with a tendency to sin — this is original sin. It is not a specific sin a person commits, but a condition inherited from the first humans.

Catholic view: Original sin is washed away through the sacrament of baptism. This is one reason Catholics baptise infants — to free the baby from original sin as early as possible. Even after baptism, humans still have a tendency to sin (called concupiscence).

Protestant view: Most Protestants accept the concept of original sin but emphasise that salvation comes through faith in Jesus rather than through sacraments. Some Protestants do not practise infant baptism, believing a person must choose to follow Christ for themselves.

Liberal view: Some liberal Christians see the story of Adam and Eve as a myth that teaches an important truth — humans have a natural tendency to do wrong — rather than a literal historical event. The lesson is the same: humans need God’s help to overcome sin.

What Is Salvation?

Salvation means being saved from sin and its consequences — ultimately, being granted eternal life with God rather than eternal separation from God. Christians believe humans cannot save themselves because all are sinful. They need God’s help.

the specification identifies three means of salvation: law, grace and Spirit. Different Christian traditions emphasise these differently.

Salvation Through Law

Some Christians believe that following God’s laws — the Ten Commandments and the moral teachings of Jesus — is essential for salvation. By obeying God’s commands, a person shows they are devoted to God and deserving of eternal life. Catholics especially emphasise the importance of good works alongside faith — the Epistle of James states: “Faith by itself, if it is not accompanied by action, is dead” (James 2:17).

Salvation Through Grace

Grace is the free, undeserved gift of God’s love. Christians believe God offers salvation not because humans deserve it, but because God loves them. Ephesians 2:8–9 states: “For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith — and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God — not by works, so that no one can boast.”

Key Fact

Protestants, especially those in the Reformed tradition, emphasise salvation by grace alone through faith alone. Humans cannot earn salvation by doing good deeds — it is a free gift from God, received through faith in Jesus Christ. Catholics believe both faith and works are necessary — grace enables good works, and both contribute to salvation.

Salvation Through the Holy Spirit

Christians believe the Holy Spirit plays an active role in salvation. The Spirit works within believers to help them recognise their sin, turn towards God, and live a holy life. Charismatic and Pentecostal Christians particularly emphasise the role of the Holy Spirit, believing it gives spiritual gifts such as speaking in tongues, prophecy and healing.

The Holy Spirit guides Christians in daily life, helping them make good decisions and resist temptation. Jesus promised: “The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things” (John 14:26). The Spirit also brings comfort in suffering, strengthens faith in difficult times, and empowers Christians to share the gospel with others.

The Role of Christ in Salvation

All Christians agree that Jesus Christ is central to salvation. Without Jesus, humans would remain trapped in sin with no way back to God. Jesus’s death and resurrection made salvation possible.

Atonement

Atonement literally means “at-one-ment” — making God and humanity “at one” again. It is the belief that Jesus’s death on the cross restored the broken relationship between God and humans caused by sin. Through his sacrifice, Jesus took the punishment that humans deserved.

Key Fact

Isaiah 53:5 prophesied the atonement: “He was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.” Christians believe this prophecy was fulfilled by Jesus on the cross.

Substitutionary atonement: Jesus took the place of sinful humans and bore the punishment they deserved. He was a substitute — dying instead of humanity. This view is common among evangelical Protestants.

Satisfaction theory: Human sin offended God’s honour and justice. Only a perfect sacrifice could satisfy God’s justice. Jesus, being sinless, was the only one who could offer this perfect payment. This view is associated with Anselm of Canterbury and is common in Catholic theology.

Moral example: Some liberal Christians see Jesus’s death less as a payment for sin and more as a supreme example of self-sacrificing love. His willingness to die inspires Christians to live selflessly and sacrificially for others.

Regardless of which understanding they hold, all Christians agree that the atonement makes salvation available. Jesus’s sacrifice opened the door for humans to be reconciled with God, forgiven for their sins, and given the promise of eternal life.

973cda2e-294f-4d4d-9b7a-92a23a13435b.title: Sin and Salvation
973cda2e-294f-4d4d-9b7a-92a23a13435b.content_html:
What Is Sin?

In Christianity, sin means any action or thought that goes against God’s will. Sin damages the relationship between humans and God. It can refer to specific wrong actions — such as lying, stealing, or harming others — but it can also describe a deeper state of being separated from God.

Most Christians believe in personal sin — when someone individually chooses to do something wrong, breaking God’s commandments. This is different from the concept of original sin, which affects all of humanity from birth.

Key Fact

Sin separates humans from God. The consequence of sin is believed to be death, but those who are saved receive eternal life.

Original Sin and the Fall

Original sin is the belief that every human is born with a built-in tendency to do wrong. The concept is generally credited to St Augustine and is an important doctrine within the Catholic Church.

According to the Book of Genesis, God placed Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden and gave them freedom to enjoy everything — except the fruit from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. A serpent tempted Eve, and both Adam and Eve ate the forbidden fruit. This act of disobedience is known as “the Fall.”

Eating the fruit made Adam and Eve aware of their own sinful act. They were cast out of paradise, and their disobedience had lasting consequences: separation from God and the introduction of death into the world. Christians believe that this damaged human nature was passed down through all their descendants. As a result, every person is born with an inherited tendency to sin.

Only Mary (Jesus’ mother) and Jesus himself are believed by Catholics to have been born without original sin. The doctrine teaches that because Adam and Eve sinned, all humans need saving — they cannot fix the problem on their own.

Key Fact

“Original sin means the first sin of Adam and Eve. They disobeyed God by eating fruit from the forbidden tree. Humans are now born with a built-in tendency to sin.” — AQA mark scheme summary

What Is Salvation?

Salvation means being saved from sin and its consequences and being granted eternal life with God. Because sin has separated humans from God, salvation is the way back — it enables humans to restore their relationship with God and receive the promise of heaven.

Christians believe that they need saving from sin so they can have a good relationship with God and avoid hell. Most Christians believe that if they put their faith in Jesus, confess their sins and ask for forgiveness, they will be saved.

How Is Salvation Achieved?

the specification identifies several means of salvation: law, grace, and the Holy Spirit. Different Christian traditions place different emphasis on each of these.

Law: In the Old Testament, Jews tried to achieve salvation by following God’s laws, including the Ten Commandments. Christians believe they no longer need to follow all of the Jewish Law because Jesus fulfilled it through his life, death and resurrection. However, many Christians still see living a moral life and doing good works as part of their response to God’s gift of salvation.

Grace: Grace is God’s unconditional love and favour, given freely to humans without them needing to earn it. Many Christians — especially Protestants — believe that salvation comes through grace alone. Jesus coming to save humanity was the ultimate expression of God’s grace. As the Bible teaches: “God so loved the world that He gave his only Son, so that whoever believes in Him shall not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16).

The Holy Spirit: Many Christians believe that they receive God’s grace through the Holy Spirit, which guides, comforts and strengthens believers in their daily lives. Christians also receive grace through the Bible, prayer and the sacraments.

Salvation by works: Some Christians believe that doing good deeds and following God’s commandments is essential for salvation. The Old Testament emphasises having faith in God and following his rules. The Parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25) suggests that people will be judged on their actions — those who helped others will enter heaven.

Salvation by faith (grace): Other Christians, particularly Protestants, believe that salvation comes through faith in Jesus Christ and God’s grace alone — not through good works. They point to passages such as “Whoever believes in me shall have eternal life” (John 6:47). Prayer and asking for forgiveness when we make mistakes are also part of receiving God’s grace.

The Role of Christ in Salvation: Atonement

Atonement is at the heart of Christian belief about salvation. It means restoring the relationship between humans and God through the life, death and resurrection of Jesus. Christians believe that Jesus’ death makes up for the original sin committed by Adam and Eve, and so brings people back to God.

As Son of God, Jesus could easily have avoided being crucified. While he was on the cross, some people shouted to him to use his power to get down. However, he knew his death was needed to restore the relationship between God and believers. This gave all people the opportunity for salvation.

Key Fact

“For since death came through a man, the resurrection of the dead also comes through a man. For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.” — 1 Corinthians 15:21–22

Jesus’ resurrection, three days after his death, showed Christians that death had been overcome and that the goodness of Jesus had defeated the power of evil. Atonement removes the effects of sin and allows people to restore their relationship with God. This is only possible because Jesus atoned for the sins of humanity when he died and rose again.

As the Bible says: “If anybody does sin, we have an advocate with the Father — Jesus Christ, the Righteous One. He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world” (1 John 2:1–2).

Atonement is important to Christians because it demonstrates God’s all-loving nature — he died for human beings so they could live with God in peace. It shows the power of good over evil and provides an example for Christians to follow. Atonement offers hope in a world full of suffering. It is remembered in the celebration of Easter and the practice of Holy Communion, and it remains the central message of Christian evangelism.

999c57bb-46c2-4d0b-9ac7-3e58592ef760.title: Tawhid and the Nature of Allah
999c57bb-46c2-4d0b-9ac7-3e58592ef760.content_html:
Tawhid — The Oneness of God

Tawhid is the single most important belief in Islam. It means the absolute oneness of Allah — there is no God but Allah, and nothing can be compared to Him. Tawhid is the foundation of everything a Muslim believes and does. It is the first part of the Shahadah (declaration of faith): “There is no God but Allah.”

Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) is the key Qur’anic text on Tawhid. It declares: “He is Allah, the One. Allah is Eternal and Absolute. None is born of Him, He is unborn. There is none like unto Him.” This short surah makes clear that Allah is unique, has always existed, was never created and cannot be compared to anything in creation.

Key Fact

Surah 112:1–4 is essential for the exam. It states that Allah is One, Eternal and Absolute, was not born and did not give birth, and nothing is comparable to Him. This surah is recited daily by Muslims and summarises the entire concept of Tawhid.

The opposite of Tawhid is Shirk — associating partners with Allah or giving God-like qualities to anything else. Shirk is considered the worst sin in Islam and the only sin Allah will not forgive. This is why Muslims do not create images of Allah or Muhammad, and why Islamic art uses geometric patterns and calligraphy rather than depictions of God.

The Nature and Qualities of Allah

Muslims believe Allah has many qualities, described throughout the Qur’an. You need to know five key attributes:

Omnipotence (Al-Qadir): Allah is all-powerful. He created the universe from nothing and sustains all life. Nothing is beyond His ability. Surah 2:20 states: “Allah has power over everything.”

Beneficence (Ar-Rahman): Allah is all-good and provides for His creation. Every surah of the Qur’an except one opens with: “In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.” Allah provides food, water, shelter and guidance for all people.

Mercy (Ar-Rahim): Allah is the Most Merciful. He forgives those who sincerely repent. Surah 39:53 says: “Do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins.” Muslims believe Allah’s mercy outweighs His wrath.

Fairness and Justice (Al-Adl): Allah treats all people fairly and never acts unjustly. Every person will be judged equally on the Day of Judgement. This quality is especially emphasised in Shi’a Islam as Adalat, one of the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din.

Justice (Adalat in Shi’a Islam): While both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims agree that Allah is just, Shi’a Islam elevates this quality to one of its core beliefs. Surah 16:90 states: “Indeed Allah commands you towards justice.” This means Allah will hold everyone accountable and will never punish the innocent.

Immanence and Transcendence

The spec asks about two contrasting ideas regarding Allah’s relationship with the world:

Transcendence means Allah is beyond and above creation. He exists outside of time, space and the physical world. Muslims emphasise that Allah is utterly different from anything humans can imagine — this is why Surah 112 says “There is none like unto Him.” Allah cannot be fully understood by the human mind.

Immanence means Allah is present and involved in the world. Despite being beyond creation, Allah is closer to every person than their own jugular vein (Surah 50:16). He hears prayers, guides individuals and intervenes in the world. Muslims experience Allah’s immanence through prayer, the Qur’an and the natural world.

Key Fact

Muslims believe Allah is both transcendent (above and beyond creation) and immanent (close and involved in the world). These ideas are not contradictory — Allah is so powerful that He can be beyond the universe and yet closer to a person than their own jugular vein (Surah 50:16).

Angels (Malaikah)

Belief in angels is the second article of Sunni faith. Malaikah are beings created by Allah from divine light (Nur). Unlike humans, angels have no free will — they obey Allah’s commands without question. Surah 35:1 describes them as “messengers with two, three, four pairs of wings.”

Jibril (Gabriel) is the most important angel. He delivered the Qur’an to the Prophet Muhammad over a period of 23 years, beginning in 610 CE during the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr). Without Jibril, Muhammad would not have received Allah’s revelation, and the Qur’an would not exist. Jibril also appeared to Ibrahim and Maryam (Mary), making him the chief messenger between Allah and humanity.

Mika’il (Michael) is the angel of mercy and provision. He is responsible for providing nourishment to human bodies and souls, and controls the natural world — rain, weather and harvest. Muslims believe Mika’il distributes Allah’s blessings throughout creation.

Angels perform several roles: they deliver revelations from Allah to prophets, they record every person’s good and bad deeds (the recording angels sit on each shoulder), they welcome the righteous into paradise, and they will be present at the Day of Judgement. The angel Israfil will blow the trumpet to announce the Day of Judgement, and Azra’il (the Angel of Death) takes souls at the moment of death.

Belief in angels influences Muslims today because it reminds them that their actions are always being recorded. This encourages moral behaviour, honesty and mindfulness in daily life. If a Muslim is tempted to do wrong, the knowledge that an angel is recording the deed acts as a powerful deterrent.

Angels are central to Islam because they connect Allah to humanity. Without Jibril, the Qur’an would not have been revealed. Without the recording angels, there would be no account of human deeds for the Day of Judgement. Belief in Malaikah therefore reinforces belief in the Qur’an, prophethood and the afterlife — linking multiple articles of faith together.

c163cb4c-004e-4b98-95eb-9647259df7da.content_html:
The Synagogue: Heart of Jewish Community Life

The synagogue is the central institution of Jewish communal life. The Hebrew word for synagogue is beit knesset — “house of assembly” — and it serves multiple purposes: a place of worship, a place of Torah study, and a community hub. Since the destruction of the Second Temple in Jerusalem in 70 CE, the synagogue has replaced the Temple as the focus of Jewish religious life. Synagogues can be found wherever there is a Jewish community — from the ancient Bevis Marks Synagogue in the City of London (built 1701, the oldest synagogue in continual use in the United Kingdom) to modern synagogues in Manchester, Leeds and every major British city.

Synagogues serve three broad functions that echo the three Hebrew terms beit knesset (assembly), beit tefillah (house of prayer) and beit midrash (house of study). Prayer services are held daily in many communities; Torah classes and adult learning take place throughout the week; life-cycle events — Bar and Bat Mitzvah, weddings, memorial services — are celebrated and marked at the synagogue. In smaller communities, the synagogue is often the sole gathering point for the entire Jewish population of a town.

Key Fact

The synagogue has three functions in Jewish life: beit knesset (house of assembly — community gathering), beit tefillah (house of prayer — worship services), and beit midrash (house of study — Torah learning). Bevis Marks Synagogue in London, established 1701, is the oldest synagogue in continuous use in the United Kingdom.

Key Features of the Synagogue

Three features of the synagogue are especially significant in Jewish worship. The bimah is the raised reading platform from which the Torah scroll is read publicly. In traditional Orthodox synagogues, the bimah stands in the centre of the main hall, reflecting the ancient Temple's design and ensuring that the congregation surrounds the reader. In most Reform synagogues, the bimah is positioned at the front of the hall, closer to the ark, emphasising the unity of the service and the rabbi’s leadership role.

The aron hakodesh — the holy ark — is the most sacred object in the synagogue. It is placed on the wall facing Jerusalem (in the UK, this means the east wall), so that the congregation faces Jerusalem when they pray. The ark houses the Torah scrolls, which are dressed in embroidered covers and adorned with silver ornaments. Opening the ark is a solemn moment in the service; the congregation rises.

Above the ark burns the ner tamid — the eternal light. This light is never extinguished, symbolising God’s constant, eternal presence. It recalls the menorah (the seven-branched lamp) which burned continuously in the ancient Temple. The ner tamid is found in both Orthodox and Reform synagogues, making it one of the universal features of Jewish worship spaces.

Orthodox and Reform Synagogues: Key Differences

The two most significant differences between Orthodox and Reform synagogues are the role of women and the language of prayer. In Orthodox synagogues, men and women sit separately: the main floor is typically reserved for men, while women sit in a separate section — either an upper gallery (a mechitza) or a partitioned area to the side. Only men may lead services and read from the Torah in Orthodox practice. Reform synagogues are fully mixed: women sit alongside men, women may be ordained as rabbis, and both men and women lead services. The West London Synagogue (opened 1840) and the Liberal Jewish Synagogue in St John’s Wood are prominent UK Reform and Liberal institutions.

Orthodox synagogue services use Hebrew almost exclusively; many prayers have been unchanged for centuries. Reform services in the UK use a mixture of Hebrew and English, with translations and explanations integrated into the service to make worship accessible to all. Reform communities also tend to have shorter services. Despite these differences, both Orthodox and Reform synagogues affirm the same central beliefs — God’s oneness, the covenant, the mitzvot — and both face Jerusalem during prayer.

Orthodox men cover their heads at all times in the synagogue (and many do so throughout the day); in Reform settings, head covering is encouraged but not always required, and women sometimes choose to wear a kippah. Orthodox services use traditional chazanut (cantorial singing) without musical instruments on Shabbat, as playing instruments is not permitted on the day of rest. Many Reform synagogues use organs or other instruments during services. The rabbi’s role differs too: Orthodox rabbis are always male and serve primarily as legal authorities and preachers; Reform communities have ordained women as rabbis since the early twentieth century in America and since the late twentieth century in the UK.

The Amidah: The Standing Prayer

The central prayer of every Jewish service is the Amidah (literally “the standing one”). It is recited three times daily — morning, afternoon and evening. During the Amidah, the worshipper stands with feet together, facing Jerusalem, and prays silently. The Amidah is divided into three sections: praise of God (three opening blessings), petitions (thirteen blessings asking for understanding, forgiveness, healing, redemption and more), and thanksgiving (three closing blessings).

The Amidah is one of the oldest prayers in Judaism, with roots in the time of the Second Temple. On Shabbat and festivals, the thirteen petitions are replaced with a single blessing for the special holiness of the day, shortening the service. The Amidah is found in both Orthodox and Reform prayer books, although Reform versions may use more inclusive language and include Hebrew alongside English translation. Its presence at the heart of every service makes it the most important regular prayer in Jewish worship.

Jewish tradition teaches that prayer should be directed towards Jerusalem and, specifically, towards the site of the Temple Mount. This is based on the prayer of Solomon at the dedication of the First Temple, which describes God as hearing prayers offered in the direction of the Temple (1 Kings 8:38-39). Even after the Temple’s destruction, the orientation towards Jerusalem expresses the Jewish longing for restoration and the continued connection to the spiritual centre of Jewish life. It also unites all Jews in prayer: wherever they are in the world, they pray in the same direction.

Key Fact

Three essential features: bimah (raised reading platform — centre in Orthodox, front in Reform); aron hakodesh (holy ark — houses Torah scrolls, faces Jerusalem); ner tamid (eternal light — above the ark, never extinguished, symbolises God’s constant presence). The Amidah is the standing prayer recited three times daily at the heart of synagogue worship.

d35f8cb8-dc25-4c27-9cc0-a965f6542158.title: Mission, Evangelism & the Worldwide Church
d35f8cb8-dc25-4c27-9cc0-a965f6542158.content_html:
The Church in the Local Community

The Church is not just a building — it is the community of believers who follow Jesus’s teachings. Christians believe they have a duty to help others in their local area. Jesus taught, “Love your neighbour as yourself” (Mark 12:31), and the Parable of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37) shows that ‘neighbour’ means anyone in need, regardless of background.

Many churches are active in their communities, running projects that support vulnerable people. Two important examples of local church action are food banks and street pastors.

Key Fact

You need to know about the Church’s role in the local community, including food banks and street pastors. These are practical examples of Christians putting Jesus’s teaching about loving your neighbour into action.

Food Banks

Food banks collect donated food and distribute it to people in crisis — those who cannot afford to feed themselves or their families. The Trussell Trust, founded on Christian principles, runs over 1,400 food bank centres across the UK. People are referred to food banks by professionals such as doctors, social workers or schools, and receive an emergency food parcel lasting three days.

Christians support food banks because Jesus taught that helping others is the same as serving God: “For I was hungry and you gave me something to eat” (Matthew 25:35). Churches provide volunteers, collection points and premises for food banks, putting their faith into practical action.

Street Pastors

Street pastors are trained Christian volunteers who patrol town and city centres at night, usually on Friday and Saturday evenings. They care for vulnerable people — offering water, flip-flops to those in bare feet, warm clothing, and a listening ear. They help people who are drunk, distressed or at risk of harm, and liaise with police and ambulance services when needed.

The Street Pastors movement was founded in London in 2003 by Reverend Les Isaac. It now operates in over 300 locations across the UK. Street pastors do not preach or try to convert people — they simply demonstrate Christian love through practical care. Their presence has been shown to reduce crime and antisocial behaviour in many areas.

Mission is the broader calling of the Church to carry out God’s work in the world. This includes preaching the gospel, caring for the poor, promoting justice and working for peace. Evangelism is the specific act of spreading the Christian faith — sharing the good news of Jesus Christ with non-believers.

Jesus commanded his followers to evangelise: “Go and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). This is known as the Great Commission. Christians carry out evangelism in many ways — through preaching, missionary work overseas, Alpha courses, social media and personal example. Church growth depends on both evangelism (reaching new people) and nurturing existing believers.

The Worldwide Church

The Church operates on a global scale. Christians believe they have a responsibility not just to their local community but to the whole world. The worldwide Church works for reconciliation (bringing peace between conflicting groups), responds to persecution, and addresses global poverty and injustice.

Reconciliation is central to Christian teaching. Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9). The worldwide Church works to bring peace in areas of conflict — for example, the role of churches in the peace process in Northern Ireland and in post-apartheid South Africa, where Archbishop Desmond Tutu led the Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

Many Christians around the world face persecution for their faith. In some countries, Christians are imprisoned, attacked or even killed for practising their religion. Churches respond by praying for persecuted Christians, raising awareness, campaigning for religious freedom and providing practical support. Jesus warned his followers that persecution would come: “If they persecuted me, they will persecute you also” (John 15:20).

CAFOD (Catholic Agency For Overseas Development) is the official Catholic aid agency for England and Wales. It works in over 40 countries, providing emergency relief after disasters, funding long-term development projects (clean water, education, healthcare) and campaigning for justice. CAFOD is funded mainly by Catholic parishes.

Christian Aid works with communities of all faiths and none in around 37 countries. It tackles poverty through emergency response, long-term development and advocacy for policy change. Christian Aid Week, held every May, raises millions of pounds through door-to-door collections and fundraising events across UK churches.

Tearfund is an evangelical Christian charity that works in over 50 countries. It partners with local churches to address poverty, provide disaster relief, and support communities in building sustainable livelihoods. Tearfund’s distinctive approach is to work through local church networks, believing that churches are uniquely placed to understand and serve their communities.

All three organisations are motivated by Jesus’s teaching to love your neighbour and care for the poor. Jesus said, “Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers and sisters of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40).

Key Fact

The specification requires knowledge of the work of one of CAFOD, Christian Aid or Tearfund. All three are motivated by Jesus’s teaching to love your neighbour (Mark 12:31) and serve the poor (Matthew 25:40), but they differ in their denominational links and methods.
