d93d9023-bbe3-40b6-81db-fca00bf1a5f0.title: Risalah, Holy Books & Prophethood
d93d9023-bbe3-40b6-81db-fca00bf1a5f0.content_html:
Risalah — Prophethood

Risalah means prophethood. Muslims believe Allah did not leave humanity without guidance — He sent prophets (messengers) at different times throughout history to teach people how to live according to His will. Prophets are human beings chosen by Allah. They are not divine, but they are considered sinless (ma’sum) and perfectly obedient to God.

The Qur’an mentions 25 prophets by name, but Muslims believe there were many more — some traditions say 124,000. Every nation received at least one prophet. The specification requires knowledge of three key prophets: Adam, Ibrahim (Abraham) and Muhammad.

Adam was the first human and the first prophet. Allah created Adam from clay and breathed life into him. Adam was placed in the Garden of Eden with Hawwa (Eve). When they disobeyed Allah by eating from the forbidden tree, they were sent to earth. However, Adam repented sincerely and Allah forgave him. In Islam, Adam is not seen as carrying “original sin” — his repentance was accepted, and every person is born sinless.

Ibrahim (Abraham) is one of the most important prophets in Islam, known as “Khalilullah” — the Friend of Allah. Ibrahim demonstrated perfect submission to God. When Allah commanded him to sacrifice his son Isma’il, Ibrahim was willing to obey, proving his total faith. Allah intervened and provided a ram instead. This event is commemorated during the festival of Id-ul-Adha. Ibrahim also rebuilt the Ka’aba in Makkah with Isma’il, establishing the site of Hajj.

Muhammad is the final and most important prophet — the “Seal of the Prophets” (Khatam an-Nabiyyin). Surah 33:40 states: “Muhammad is… the messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets.” This means no more prophets will come after him. Muhammad received the Qur’an from the angel Jibril over 23 years, beginning in 610 CE. His life and teachings (the Hadith) are a model for all Muslims to follow. Muhammad’s example is known as the Sunnah.

Key Fact

Muhammad is called the “Seal of the Prophets” (Surah 33:40), meaning he is the last and final messenger of Allah. No new prophets will come after him. His message — the Qur’an — is considered the complete and final revelation from God.

The Holy Books (Kutub)

Muslims believe Allah revealed His guidance through several holy books, each given to a different prophet. Belief in these books is the third article of Sunni faith (Kutub). However, Muslims believe that all previous scriptures were either lost, altered or corrupted over time. Only the Qur’an remains in its original, unchanged form.

The Qur’an was revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril over 23 years. It contains 114 surahs (chapters) and is considered the literal, unchanged word of Allah in Arabic. It is the supreme authority in Islam — every other source of guidance is secondary to it. Muslims treat the physical Qur’an with great respect: it is kept on the highest shelf, hands are washed before reading it, and nothing is placed on top of it.

The Torah (Tawrat) was revealed to the Prophet Musa (Moses). It contained Allah’s laws and guidance for the Israelites.

The Psalms (Zabur) were revealed to the Prophet Dawud (David). They contained hymns and praises to Allah.

The Gospel (Injil) was revealed to the Prophet Isa (Jesus). It contained guidance and teachings from Allah for the people of that time.

The Scrolls of Abraham (Suhuf Ibrahim) were among the earliest revelations, given to the Prophet Ibrahim. They have been lost entirely.

Key Fact

The Qur’an has supreme authority in Islam because Muslims believe it is the only holy book that has never been changed or corrupted. It is the direct word of Allah, revealed in Arabic through Jibril, and it supersedes all previous scriptures.

The Qur’an: Revelation and Authority

The Qur’an was revealed to Muhammad beginning on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr) in approximately 610 CE. Muhammad was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira near Makkah when the angel Jibril appeared and commanded him to “Read!” (Surah 96:1–5). Muhammad could not read, but the words were pressed into his heart. Revelations continued for the next 23 years until Muhammad’s death in 632 CE.

The Qur’an’s authority in Islam is absolute. It is the primary source of Shari’ah (Islamic law) and provides guidance on worship, morality, family life, justice and social conduct. When a question arises, Muslims turn first to the Qur’an, then to the Hadith and Sunnah, and then to scholarly interpretation.

The Imamate in Shi’a Islam

The Imamate is the fourth root of Usul ad-Din and is unique to Shi’a Islam. Shi’a Muslims believe that after Muhammad’s death, leadership of the Muslim community should have passed to his cousin and son-in-law Ali, and then through a line of twelve Imams descended from Muhammad’s family (Ahl al-Bayt).

Divine appointment: Shi’a Muslims believe each Imam was chosen by Allah, not elected by the community. This gives them a religious authority that Sunni caliphs did not claim.

Infallibility: The Imams are considered ma’sum (sinless and infallible). They cannot make mistakes in matters of faith and are perfect interpreters of the Qur’an and Islamic law.

The Twelfth Imam: Shi’a Muslims believe the twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, went into “occultation” (hiding) in 874 CE. He is believed to be alive and will return at the end of time as a messianic figure to establish justice and peace on earth.

Influence today: Because the twelfth Imam is in hiding, Shi’a scholars (ayatollahs and mujtahids) act as his representatives, interpreting Islamic law on his behalf. This gives senior Shi’a clergy a level of religious authority that has no parallel in Sunni Islam.

The Imamate is a key difference between Sunni and Shi’a Islam. Sunni Muslims do not believe in divinely appointed, infallible leaders after Muhammad. They followed elected caliphs and rely on scholarly consensus for interpretation of Islamic law. For Shi’a Muslims, the Imamate is not merely a political institution — it is a core theological belief about how Allah continues to guide humanity.

eeaf84d6-a61c-40bc-9cbd-4e72ddbbbf16.title: Moral Principles, Mitzvot and Pikuach Nefesh
eeaf84d6-a61c-40bc-9cbd-4e72ddbbbf16.content_html:
Jewish Moral Principles: An Overview

Judaism is often described as a religion of action. Beliefs matter deeply, but what Jewish teaching emphasises above all else is how people treat one another and how they respond to God’s call to live justly. The mitzvot are not experienced by most Jews as burdensome restrictions but as a framework of sanctity — a way of bringing holiness into every moment of daily life. Jewish tradition teaches that no mitzvah is too small to matter: even feeding a hungry person or speaking honestly in a business deal is an act of worship.

Four core moral principles run through Jewish ethical teaching and appear explicitly in the Torah and the prophetic tradition: tzedek (justice), tikkun olam (healing the world), tzedakah (charity) and chesed (loving kindness). These four principles operate together and are reflected in countless practical mitzvot.

Tzedek: Justice

The Hebrew word tzedek means both “justice” and “righteousness.” The Torah commands, “Justice, justice shall you pursue” (Deuteronomy 16:20) — the double repetition of the word signals its urgency. Jewish courts (batei din) have a long tradition of applying Torah law to resolve disputes fairly. The prophets of the Tenakh — particularly Amos, Micah and Isaiah — repeatedly challenged the wealthy and powerful to treat the poor justly, warning that God is not satisfied with ritual worship when justice is absent from public life. “Let justice roll down like waters and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream” (Amos 5:24).

Tzedakah: Charity as Obligation

Tzedakah is often translated as “charity” but the Hebrew root is tzedek (justice) — giving to the poor is understood not as an act of generosity but as an act of justice. The poor have a right to a portion of the community’s resources; the wealthy have an obligation to give. Many Jewish communities have a tzedakah box (pushke) in the home into which small amounts are placed regularly, making giving a habitual part of daily life. Organisations such as World Jewish Relief operate from this principle, providing aid to vulnerable people across the world regardless of religion.

A common error is to describe the 613 mitzvot as “rules Jews have to follow.” Jewish teaching frames the mitzvot very differently: they are not restrictions imposed from outside but a gift from God — a detailed guide to living a sanctified life. Observant Jews describe the sense of meaning and structure the mitzvot bring to daily life. Keeping Shabbat is not experienced as a ban on work; it is experienced as a weekly gift of rest and family togetherness. This is the texture the exam rewards: mitzvot as joyful duties and expressions of the covenant, not as arbitrary rules.

Tikkun Olam: Healing the World

The concept of tikkun olam — repair or healing of the world — has become one of the most widely cited principles of Jewish ethics in the modern period, particularly in Reform and Liberal communities. It expresses the idea that the world as it is is not as it should be: there is suffering, injustice and brokenness. Every act of justice, every act of tzedakah, every act of chesed is a stitch in the repair of the world. Modern Jewish organisations that campaign for human rights, environmental justice or refugee support often invoke tikkun olam as their motivating principle. Jewish Care and HIAS (the Hebrew Immigrant Aid Society) are examples in Britain and internationally.

The Sanctity of Human Life and Pikuach Nefesh

One of the most distinctive and powerful teachings in Judaism is Pikuach Nefesh — the principle that preserving human life takes precedence over almost all of the commandments. The Talmud teaches that to save a single life is as if one has saved an entire world (Sanhedrin 37a). This remarkable teaching reflects the absolute sanctity of every human being, created in the image of God (tzelem Elohim).

In practice, Pikuach Nefesh means that if a life is at risk, a Jew is obligated to break Shabbat rules, eat non-kosher food, or disregard almost any other commandment in order to save that life. Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Jews all affirm this principle, though they may apply it differently in edge cases. Medical professionals in the Jewish community may work on Shabbat; an ambulance driver who is Jewish will drive to save a life. The principle shows that the mitzvot serve human life — they are never more important than life itself.

Key Fact

Pikuach Nefesh: preserving human life overrides almost all of the 613 mitzvot. Rooted in the teaching that every person is created in God’s image (tzelem Elohim) and that “one who saves a single life, it is as if they have saved an entire world” (Talmud, Sanhedrin 37a). This principle is accepted across Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism.

Free Will and the Mitzvot

Jewish teaching holds that God gave human beings genuine free will. The mitzvot are binding obligations, but no one is compelled to observe them. The Torah presents the choice explicitly: “I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse; therefore choose life” (Deuteronomy 30:19). The fact that God requires observance of the mitzvot but does not compel it makes every act of obedience or disobedience morally significant.

The tension between free will and divine commandment is one that Jewish thinkers have explored across the centuries. If God knows in advance what each person will choose, how is that choice truly free? Maimonides wrote that “free will is given to every human being” and that God’s foreknowledge does not remove human moral responsibility — a teaching maintained across Orthodox, Reform and Liberal Judaism today.

Chesed — loving kindness — is expressed in countless ways in British Jewish community life. A large Reform synagogue in north-west London runs a weekly food bank and visits housebound elderly members; the young people’s group at a Manchester Reform synagogue organises clothing collections for asylum seekers. These acts are understood not simply as “volunteering” but as performing a mitzvah — fulfilling a divine commandment to show kindness to others. The distinction matters: chesed is not optional generosity but a religious obligation rooted in the covenant relationship with God.

Key Fact

The four core Jewish moral principles: Tzedek (justice — pursue fair treatment for all); Tikkun olam (repair the world — act to reduce suffering and injustice); Tzedakah (charity — giving as a moral obligation, not optional generosity); Chesed (loving kindness — showing compassion to all, especially the vulnerable).

07cdf80f-7c3c-467f-ab01-063fcf13ddb4.title: Akhand Path, Langar and Nam Japna
07cdf80f-7c3c-467f-ab01-063fcf13ddb4.content_html:
The Akhand Path

The akhand path is one of the most distinctive and demanding practices in Sikhism. It is the continuous, unbroken reading of the entire Guru Granth Sahib from beginning to end — all 1,430 pages. This takes approximately 48 hours. The reading is divided between a series of readers who take turns, with no gaps in the recitation. At no point is the reading paused or interrupted; when one reader finishes their section, the next begins immediately, even in the middle of the night.

The akhand path is performed to mark significant occasions — festivals such as Vaisakhi and Gurpurbs, major lifecycle events such as the naming ceremony of a new baby or a marriage, occasions of national or community significance, or times of grief. For many Sikh families, beginning a major life event with an akhand path is a way of placing the whole event under the guidance of the eternal Guru. The reading is typically concluded so that the final words are read at a specific time — for a wedding, for example, it ends just before the ceremony begins.

Key Fact

The akhand path is the continuous, unbroken reading of the entire Guru Granth Sahib, taking approximately 48 hours. It is performed at festivals, major life events and times of community significance, placing the occasion under the living Guru’s guidance.

Langar: The Free Communal Kitchen

Langar is the free communal kitchen and meal served at every gurdwara. The word can refer both to the kitchen itself and to the meal it provides. Every person who enters a gurdwara is welcome to eat at the langar, free of charge, with no questions asked. There is no distinction based on religion, caste, ethnicity, social class or gender.

The institution of langar was established by Guru Nanak and developed through the ten Gurus. Guru Amar Das (the third Guru) made it mandatory for visitors to eat in the langar before seeking an audience with him — including, famously, the Mughal Emperor Akbar, who sat on the floor and ate simple vegetarian food alongside everyone else. This was a deliberate, public act of equality.

Langar is understood as an expression of sewa. Preparing and serving the food is tan sewa (physical service); donating ingredients or money to fund the langar is dhan sewa (material service). All volunteers who work in the langar — chopping vegetables, cooking, washing dishes, serving meals — are performing worship. At the Golden Temple (Harimandir Sahib) in Amritsar, the langar serves over 100,000 meals every day, operated entirely by volunteers. At the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall, thousands of meals are served every week.

The langar is traditionally served as vegetarian food so that people of every faith can eat together. Since religious dietary restrictions vary widely — Muslims require halal meat; Jews require kosher food; Hindus may not eat beef; many Buddhists are vegetarian — vegetarian food allows the langar to be truly open to all. This is a practical expression of the Sikh teaching that all people are equal and all are welcome. The Rehat Maryada (the Sikh code of conduct, formalised in 1945) confirms that the langar should be vegetarian. Some amritdhari Sikhs also abstain from meat entirely as a personal spiritual discipline, though this is not a universal Sikh requirement.

Nam Japna: Meditating on the Name of God

Nam japna (also written nam simran) is the practice of meditating on or repeating the name of God. The word nam means “name” (of God) and japna means “to recite” or “to meditate on.” It is one of the three pillars of Sikh teaching alongside honest work (kirat karni) and sharing with others (vand chakna).

Nam japna is practised both individually and communally. In the gurdwara, it takes the form of kirtan — devotional singing of hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib, led by musicians (ragis) playing traditional instruments including the harmonium and tabla. The congregation listens and joins in. Kirtan is understood as a communal form of nam japna — the entire sangat meditating on God’s name through music.

In daily life, nam japna takes the form of the Nitnem — the daily prayers observed by amritdhari Sikhs, beginning with the recitation of Japji Sahib (composed by Guru Nanak) in the early morning. Many Sikh families begin the day by listening to or reciting the Japji Sahib before sunrise. The name most commonly used in nam japna is Waheguru (Wondrous Lord), which may be repeated silently or aloud, alone or in a group, at any time of day.

Guru Nanak taught that the most direct path to mukti (liberation) is through sincere, constant remembrance of God’s name. The Guru Granth Sahib teaches that the mind that turns away from God becomes restless, distracted and vulnerable to the five vices. But the mind that continually returns to Waheguru through nam japna gradually stills the ego (haumai) and opens itself to God’s grace. In this sense, nam japna is not merely a ritual but the fundamental orientation of the gurmukh’s life — the spiritual thread that runs through all other practices, from sewa in the langar to sitting in the sangat during kirtan.

Key Fact

Nam japna is the most direct path to mukti in Guru Nanak’s teaching. Repeating or meditating on Waheguru — in the morning Nitnem, during kirtan, or silently throughout the day — stills the ego, opens the soul to God’s grace, and directly counteracts haumai (self-centredness).

19834c39-90f1-44b7-afb6-78b50a3d8487.title: Abortion and Euthanasia
19834c39-90f1-44b7-afb6-78b50a3d8487.content_html:
Abortion

Abortion is the deliberate termination of a pregnancy. It remains one of the most debated moral issues in modern society. Before 1967, abortion was illegal in the UK, and women resorted to dangerous “back street” abortions that led to infections, injuries, and deaths.

Key Fact

Under the 1990 Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act, abortion is legal in the UK up to 24 weeks if two doctors agree that at least one condition applies: the mother’s life is at risk, there is risk to her physical or mental health, there is a significant chance the baby would be born with severe disabilities, or an additional child would affect the wellbeing of existing children.

Christian Views on Abortion

Christians hold a range of views on abortion, but all agree that human life has special value because it is created by God.

The Roman Catholic Church teaches that abortion is always wrong. Catholics believe life begins at conception and that destroying a foetus is equivalent to murder. This is rooted in the sanctity of life — the idea that life is sacred because God created it. The Bible states: “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). Catholics apply this directly to abortion.

The Bible also suggests God has a plan for every life before birth: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born I set you apart” (Jeremiah 1:5). Psalm 139:13 adds: “For you created my inmost being; you knit me together in my mother’s womb.”

However, other Christians, including many Anglicans and Methodists, believe abortion may be acceptable in certain circumstances. Jesus taught that the most important thing is love (agape), and it may be the most loving action to allow abortion if the mother’s life is at risk or the pregnancy resulted from rape. As Colossians 3:12 says: “Clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, gentleness and patience.”

Pro-life supporters believe the foetus has a right to life from conception and that abortion is morally wrong. They argue adoption is always an alternative. Pro-choice supporters believe a woman should have the right to decide what happens to her own body. They argue that a foetus is not yet a person, especially in early pregnancy, and that forcing a woman to continue an unwanted pregnancy can cause serious harm.

Islamic Views on Abortion

Muslims believe human life is precious because it is given by Allah. The Qur’an teaches: “Do not kill your children for fear of poverty — We shall provide for them and for you — killing them is a great sin” (Qur’an 17:31). This verse is widely used to argue that abortion for financial reasons is haram (forbidden).

A key concept in Islam is ensoulment — the moment when the foetus receives its soul from Allah. Many scholars place this at 120 days after conception. Before ensoulment, some Muslims believe abortion may be permitted if the mother’s life is in danger. After ensoulment, abortion is generally forbidden because the foetus is considered a living being with a soul.

The Qur’an also warns: “If anyone kills a person — unless in retribution for murder or spreading corruption in the land — it is as if he kills all mankind” (Qur’an 5:32). Most Muslims agree that the mother’s life takes priority over the life of the foetus.

Euthanasia

Euthanasia comes from the Greek words eu (good) and thanatos (death), meaning “a good death.” All forms of euthanasia are currently illegal in the UK and treated as murder or manslaughter.

Key Fact

Active euthanasia is taking deliberate action to end a life, such as giving a lethal injection. Passive euthanasia is allowing someone to die by withdrawing or withholding treatment. Voluntary euthanasia is when the patient requests death. Non-voluntary euthanasia is when the patient cannot give consent, for example because they are in a coma.

Tony Bland was 18 when he attended the Hillsborough football stadium in 1989. A crush resulted in 97 deaths and left Tony in a persistent vegetative state (PVS) with irreversible brain damage. Although there was no hope of recovery, he was kept alive through tubes providing food and fluids. In 1993, the hospital and his parents obtained court permission to withdraw treatment. Tony became the first patient in UK legal history to be allowed to die through the withdrawal of life-prolonging treatment. The law did not classify this as passive euthanasia.

In September 2015, the British Parliament rejected plans for a “right to die” law in England and Wales. 118 MPs voted in favour and 330 against allowing terminally ill adults to end their lives with medical supervision. In countries such as Belgium and the Netherlands, euthanasia is legal under strict conditions — the patient must request it, their suffering must be unbearable, and two doctors must be consulted.

Christian Views on Euthanasia

Most Christians oppose euthanasia because of the sanctity of life. The Ten Commandments state “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13), and Psalm 139:16 teaches that God has ordained every day of a person’s life. The Salvation Army has stated: “All people deserve compassion and care in suffering and dying. Euthanasia and assisted suicide should not, however, be considered acceptable responses. They undermine human dignity and are morally wrong.”

However, some Christians accept the principle of double effect — where medicine given to relieve pain may shorten life as a side effect. They see this as different from intentional killing because the primary intention is to reduce suffering, not to cause death. Many Christians actively support hospice care and palliative care as compassionate alternatives to euthanasia. Jesus taught “Blessed are the merciful” (Matthew 5:7), and Christians apply this by caring for the dying with dignity.

For: People deserve to die with dignity. If someone’s quality of life is very low, it may be more compassionate to let them die. Everyone should have the right to decide how they die. Against: Someone might recover. It is a “slippery slope” that could lead to abuse. No one should carry the burden of deciding another person’s death. It devalues the sanctity of life. As Dr Gunning warned: “Once you accept killing as a solution to a single problem, you will find tomorrow hundreds of problems for which killing can be seen as a solution.”

Islamic Views on Euthanasia

Islam is firmly opposed to all forms of euthanasia. Muslims believe in predestination — that Allah has planned every person’s life, and to end life prematurely is to interfere with His plan. The Qur’an states: “No soul may die except with God’s permission at a predestined time” (Qur’an 3:145), and “Do not kill each other, for God is merciful to you” (Qur’an 4:29).

Key Fact

Euthanasia is haram in Islam. Muslims believe all life is a gift from Allah and only Allah decides when it ends. Suffering may be a test of faith, and caring for the sick is an opportunity to do good that helps a person gain entry to paradise. Unlike some Christians, most Muslim scholars reject even the principle of double effect.

202ba232-55ea-4a04-a061-38c14db5e195.title: Death, Funeral Rites and Festivals
202ba232-55ea-4a04-a061-38c14db5e195.content_html:
Buddhist Beliefs About Death

Buddhist teaching holds that death is not an ending but a transition. Because there is no permanent, fixed self (anatta), what continues from one life to the next is not a “soul” in the Western sense but a stream of consciousness shaped by the moral quality of previous intentional actions (kamma). The dying moment is considered particularly significant: the mental state and intentions at the point of death create the conditions for the next birth. This is why, in many Buddhist traditions, loved ones recite texts, chant or create a calm and focused environment at the deathbed — to support the dying person’s mental state at this critical transition.

The ultimate goal remains liberation from the cycle of rebirth (samsara). For Theravada Buddhism, attaining nibbana means the stream of consciousness does not take rebirth after death. For Mahayana Buddhism, the Bodhisattva may choose to be reborn to help others, and Pure Land Buddhism teaches that sincere devotion to Amitabha Buddha can bring rebirth in the Pure Land.

Theravada Death and Funeral Rites

In Theravada communities (common in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Burma, Cambodia and among South Asian Buddhist communities in Britain), funeral rites emphasise monks, chanting and the transfer of merit. When a Theravada Buddhist dies, monks are invited to chant suttas from the Pali Canon at the home or at a vihara. This chanting is understood to benefit both the deceased — supporting a good rebirth — and the living, who gain merit by offering hospitality and dana (generosity) to the monks.

Cremation is the traditional practice in most Theravada communities, following the example of the Buddha, whose body was cremated after his parinibbana (final nibbana/death). The family typically performs meritorious acts in the deceased’s name — donating to the vihara, feeding monks, offering robes — and merit is “transferred” to the deceased, understood as helping their next birth. Mourning periods typically last several days, with chanting continuing throughout.

In Japan, Buddhist funeral rites are deeply embedded in social culture: the majority of Japanese funerals are conducted in Buddhist style, even among families with limited formal Buddhist practice. The deceased is often given a posthumous Buddhist name (kaimyo) and a funeral ceremony conducted by a Buddhist priest. The body is cremated, and the ashes are interred in a family grave. Memorial services are held on prescribed days after death — the seventh day, the forty-ninth day (particularly significant as it marks the end of the bardic or transitional state in some traditions), and annually on the death anniversary. Incense, chanting and offerings of food and flowers accompany these ceremonies. Japanese Buddhist funerals combine Pure Land, Zen and other Mahayana traditions in forms specific to each temple and family lineage.

Tibetan Buddhism has one of the most elaborate systems of death rites in any religious tradition. The Bardo Thodol (known in the West as the “Tibetan Book of the Dead”) is read aloud to or near the dying and newly dead person to guide their consciousness through the bardo — the intermediate state between death and rebirth. The text describes a series of experiences after death, beginning with a flash of clear light representing the true nature of mind. A practitioner who recognises this light may attain liberation; if not, they encounter a sequence of visions and eventually take rebirth according to their kamma. Lamas (teachers) may perform specific rituals over several days or weeks to support the deceased’s transition. Sky burial (the body left on a mountaintop for birds) is the traditional Tibetan method; cremation is also used for high lamas. Tibetan Buddhist communities in Britain, such as at Samye Ling Tibetan Monastery in Scotland, have adapted these practices for a British context.

Wesak: The Buddha’s Birthday

Wesak (also written Vesak or Vesākha) is the most widely observed Buddhist festival worldwide. For most Theravada Buddhists, the full moon of May commemorates all three of the Buddha’s most significant life events on a single day: his birth in Lumbini, his Enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, and his parinibbana (final nibbana/death) at Kushinara. This “three-in-one” significance is unique to Wesak and explains its weight in Buddhist devotional life.

In Britain today, Buddhist communities celebrate Wesak with processions, lantern displays, communal meals and meditation sessions. The Wat Buddhapadipa Thai Buddhist temple in Wimbledon, London, hosts one of the largest Wesak celebrations in the UK. At Wesak, Buddhists make offerings at the temple, participate in chanting, hear Dhamma talks, and engage in acts of merit and generosity (dana) — feeding the poor, releasing captive animals and performing acts of kindness.

Key Fact

Wesak: celebrated on the full moon of May; marks the birth, Enlightenment and parinibbana of the Buddha; the most important Buddhist festival globally. Parinirvana Day: observed on 15 February (in most Mahayana traditions); marks the death of the Buddha — his final entry into nibbana; a time for reflection on impermanence and the transience of life.

Key Fact

Both Wesak and Parinirvana Day connect Buddhist practitioners in Britain to the life and teaching of the historical Buddha. Wesak (full moon of May) is the most widely observed Buddhist festival globally; Parinirvana Day (15 February) is primarily a Mahayana observance. Together they frame the whole arc of the Buddha's life — from birth to Enlightenment to death — as the pattern for Buddhist practice.

Parinirvana Day

Parinirvana Day (also called Nirvana Day) is observed primarily by Mahayana Buddhist communities. It marks the day the Buddha died — his final entry into parinibbana at Kushinara at the age of approximately eighty. For Mahayana Buddhists, this is a solemn occasion for meditation and reflection on the teaching of impermanence (anicca). If even the Buddha — who had attained Enlightenment — was subject to the death of the physical body, this is a vivid reminder that all conditioned existence is transient.

Buddhist centres across Britain mark Parinirvana Day with meditation sessions, Dhamma talks, and readings from texts recording the Buddha’s final instructions to his disciples. One of his last teachings, as recorded in the Tipitaka, urged his followers: “All conditioned things are impermanent. Strive for your liberation with diligence.” Parinirvana Day thus reinforces the core teaching of anicca and the urgency of the Buddhist path.

24325c7e-1798-4a94-aec7-5343cc8ac4a0.title: War: Just War, Holy War & Pacifism
24325c7e-1798-4a94-aec7-5343cc8ac4a0.content_html:
Reasons for War

War is an armed conflict between two or more sides, usually nations or organised groups. There are many reasons why wars begin, but the three main reasons studied in GCSE Religious Studies are greed, self-defence and retaliation.

Greed drives wars fought for power, territory or resources. Many governments disguise greed as other motivations, but religious believers generally consider greed an unjust reason for war. Self-defence is widely accepted as a legitimate reason for fighting — both Christians and Muslims agree that protecting yourself and others from harm is justified. Retaliation means fighting back as revenge for a previous attack. While it can deter future aggression, religious believers warn that retaliation often creates a cycle of violence.

Just War Theory

The just war theory was developed by Christian thinkers, most notably St Thomas Aquinas in the 13th century, to determine when fighting a war could be morally acceptable. It recognises that while peace is always preferable, there are circumstances where war may be the lesser evil.

Key Fact

The criteria for a just war include: (1) it must be fought for a just cause, such as self-defence; (2) it must be declared by a legitimate authority, such as a government; (3) the intention must be to promote good and overcome evil; (4) war must be a last resort, after all peaceful alternatives have been exhausted; (5) there must be a reasonable chance of success; (6) proportional force must be used — no more violence than is necessary; (7) civilians must not be deliberately targeted.

Most mainstream Christian denominations accept the just war theory. The Catholic Church teaches that governments have a right and duty to defend their citizens, provided the strict conditions of a just war are met. The Church of England also supports the just war approach, arguing that there are times when failing to act would cause greater suffering.

However, Jesus’s own teaching emphasises peace and non-violence. He said: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44) and “All who draw the sword will die by the sword” (Matthew 26:52). This creates a tension within Christianity between the ideal of peace and the practical reality that war may sometimes be necessary.

Holy War

A holy war is a war fought for a religious cause or believed to be commanded by God. In Christianity, the Crusades (11th–13th centuries) are the most well-known example — European Christians fought to recapture the Holy Land from Muslim control. In Islam, the concept of lesser jihad permits armed struggle to defend Islam, but only under strict conditions.

For a holy war to be legitimate in Islam, it must be declared by a recognised religious authority, be fought in self-defence (not aggression), use proportionate force, and not target civilians, the elderly, women or children. The Qur’an states: “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not like transgressors” (2:190).

Key Fact

Just war vs holy war: A just war uses moral criteria to decide if a war is acceptable — it does not have to be religious. A holy war is fought specifically for a religious cause. Today, most Christian and Muslim leaders reject the idea of holy war, arguing that religion should not be used to justify violence.

Pacifism

Pacifism is the belief that all violence and war is wrong, regardless of the circumstances. Pacifists argue that conflicts should always be resolved through dialogue, negotiation and peaceful protest.

The strongest pacifist tradition in Christianity comes from the Quakers (Society of Friends), who believe that all war is wrong. They follow Jesus’s teaching to “turn the other cheek” (Matthew 5:39) literally and refuse to fight in any conflict. Many Quakers served as conscientious objectors during the World Wars, working as ambulance drivers or in hospitals instead.

Islam does not have a strong pacifist tradition in the same way. The Qur’an permits self-defence, and Muhammad himself participated in battles to protect the early Muslim community. However, many Muslims emphasise that Islam means “peace” and that the greater jihad — the internal struggle to be a good Muslim — is more important than any physical conflict.

Religion as a Cause of War

Religion has been cited as a cause of conflict throughout history — from the Crusades to modern-day conflicts in the Middle East. However, many scholars argue that religion is rarely the sole cause of war. Most conflicts involve a complex mix of political, economic and territorial factors, with religion sometimes used to justify violence rather than being its root cause.

Both Christians and Muslims argue that their faith promotes peace, not war. Where religious violence occurs, leaders from both traditions condemn it. Pope Francis has stated that “war is always a defeat for humanity,” and Muslim scholars worldwide have signed declarations condemning violence carried out in the name of Islam.

Christianity: Quakers take an absolute pacifist position, rejecting all violence. Most other Christian denominations accept that war may sometimes be necessary (just war theory) but should always be a last resort. All Christians agree that Jesus taught peace and non-violence as the ideal.

Islam: Most Muslims are not pacifists in the absolute sense. The Qur’an permits self-defence, and Muhammad fought to protect the Muslim community. However, peace is the preferred state, and the greater jihad (inner spiritual struggle) is considered more important than the lesser jihad (armed conflict). Some individual Muslims, such as Abdul Ghaffar Khan, have adopted pacifist positions inspired by their faith.

384d8d12-3ca1-4840-9cee-423a579aa92d.title: Worship at Home and the Mandir
384d8d12-3ca1-4840-9cee-423a579aa92d.content_html:
Where Do Hindus Worship?

Hindu teaching holds that the divine is present everywhere — in the home, the temple, the natural world and, most profoundly, within the heart of every individual. This understanding means that worship (puja in its broadest sense) is not limited to a special building or a weekly appointment, but is woven into daily life.

The four places of worship are: the home, the temple (mandir), outdoors (including natural shrines), and the space of the heart. Each has its own character and importance, and in British Hindu life all four are actively used.

The Home Shrine

For most Hindu families in Britain, the home is the primary place of daily worship. Almost every Hindu home has a dedicated sacred space — a shelf, a cabinet or a whole room — known as the puja room or home shrine. Here, images or statues of deities (murtis) are kept, along with incense, oil lamps (diyas), flowers and other offerings.

Nalini, a 52-year-old Vaishnavite Hindu in Coventry, begins every day at 6am at her home shrine. She offers flowers to a murti of Krishna, lights a diya, recites a mantra and performs a short arati. “It sets the tone for the whole day,” she says. “I am reminding myself of what is truly real before the busy world begins.” This daily domestic ritual is a central expression of Hindu devotion in Britain today.

The Mandir: Temple Worship

The mandir (temple) is understood as the house of God. The most prominent Hindu temple in the UK is the BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir in Neasden, London — the largest Hindu temple outside India — built entirely from hand-carved limestone and marble by craftsmen following ancient temple-building principles. When a worshipper enters the mandir, they remove their shoes as a sign of respect, signalling that they are entering sacred ground.

Central to temple worship is darshan: the auspicious sight of the divine through the murti. Hindus come to the mandir not primarily to hear a sermon but to “see and be seen by” the deity. The gaze of the murti is considered a living transmission of divine blessing. In a large mandir, worshippers will queue to stand before the consecrated image and receive darshan.

Key Fact

Four places: home shrine, mandir (temple), outdoors/natural shrines, the space of the heart. Key forms of worship: puja, arati, darshan, havan, bhajan/kirtan, japa/mantra.

Key Fact

The BAPS Shri Swaminarayan Mandir in Neasden, London, is the largest Hindu temple outside India. It was built entirely from hand-carved Turkish limestone and Italian marble, without the use of steel, following ancient Vedic Shilpa Shastra building principles. Over 3,000 volunteers helped during its construction, illustrating how the mandir functions as a community expression of devotion as well as a place of worship.

Forms of Worship: Puja, Arati and Havan

Puja is the central act of Hindu worship. At home or in the mandir, puja involves a sequence of offerings to the deity: water for washing, flowers, incense, food (prasad), a flame and sometimes cloth. Each offering honours a different aspect of the deity and the worshipper’s relationship with the divine. Puja creates a sacred transaction — the devotee offers love and honour; the deity offers blessing and presence in return.

Arati is the waving of a flame (typically in a multi-wicked lamp called a thali or aarti dish) before a murti. It is accompanied by the singing of devotional hymns. The flame symbolises divine light illuminating the worshipper’s life. After arati, worshippers bring their hands over the flame and then to their face — symbolically receiving the divine light.

Havan (also called yajna) is a fire ritual. Offerings of ghee (clarified butter), grains and sometimes specific herbs are made into a consecrated fire while Sanskrit mantras are recited. Havan is one of the oldest forms of Hindu worship, rooted in the Vedic tradition. It is performed at key life events (weddings, naming ceremonies, housewarmings) and at special temple occasions.

Bhajan, Kirtan, Japa and Mantra

Bhajan and kirtan are devotional singing. Bhajans are devotional songs praising a deity; kirtan is the communal, call-and-response chanting of divine names or scripture. Both are considered acts of bhakti (devotion) and are especially beloved in Vaishnavite communities. The ISKCON community at Bhaktivedanta Manor (near Watford) is well known for its joyful public kirtan.

Japa is the meditative repetition of a divine name or mantra. It is typically counted on a mala (a string of 108 beads, corresponding to the 108 names of God). The most famous japa in Vaishnavite tradition is the Hare Krishna maha-mantra; Shaivite Hindus may repeat the name of Shiva (“Om Namah Shivaya”). A mantra is a sacred sound or phrase believed to carry spiritual potency. Mantras may be in Sanskrit and are received from a teacher (guru).

While the forms of worship — puja, arati, bhajan, japa — are broadly shared, the focus of devotion differs between Hindu sub-traditions. Vaishnavite worship centres on Vishnu, Krishna or Rama. The Bhagavad Gita’s emphasis on loving devotion to a personal God makes bhakti the heart of Vaishnavite practice. Vaishnavite mandirs display images of Krishna, Rama, Lakshmi and Vishnu; the maha-mantra (“Hare Krishna”) is central to japa. Shaivite worship centres on Shiva. The Shiva lingam — an abstract form representing Shiva’s divine energy — is the central sacred object in Shaivite temples. Shaivite puja may involve the ritual bathing (abhisheka) of the lingam with water, milk and honey. The mantra “Om Namah Shivaya” is widely used for japa. Both traditions use the same forms of worship (puja, arati, mantra), but their specific prayers, images and theological emphasis differ significantly.

Outdoor worship takes many forms. Natural features — rivers (especially the Ganges in India), hilltops, sacred trees and rocks — are recognised as places where the divine is particularly present. In Britain, some Hindus gather at outdoor events for festivals such as Holi. The Bhagavad Gita and the Upanishads both speak of the divine as present in every element of nature. The “space of the heart” refers to the innermost place of consciousness where, according to Hindu teaching, God dwells within every individual. Advanced meditation is understood as entering this inner sanctuary — the most immediate encounter with the divine possible.

39be2f8f-86f3-471e-a47b-d1d7a74ed1f8.title: Festivals, Birth and Naming Ceremonies
39be2f8f-86f3-471e-a47b-d1d7a74ed1f8.content_html:
Festivals in Sikh Life

Sikh festivals are called melas (gatherings or fairs) and Gurpurbs (Guru anniversaries). Together they mark the cycle of the Sikh year and connect the community to its history, scripture and values. For Sikhs in Britain, festivals are celebrated both at local gurdwaras and, for some families, through visits to India and historically significant gurdwaras.

Vaisakhi (Baisakhi)

Vaisakhi (also spelled Baisakhi) is celebrated in April and is one of the most important festivals in the Sikh calendar. Its religious significance is paramount: it was at Vaisakhi in 1699 that Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, calling five men from different castes to offer their lives for their faith and initiating them into the first Khalsa brotherhood. This moment is seen as the birth of the Khalsa and a defining moment in Sikh history.

In Britain, Vaisakhi is celebrated with akhand paths in the days leading up to the festival, processions (nagar kirtan) through city streets, kirtan in the gurdwara, langar, and in recent years large public celebrations in cities including Southall, Birmingham and Glasgow. The nagar kirtan is led by the Panj Pyare (five initiated Sikhs who symbolise the original Five Beloved Ones), carrying the Guru Granth Sahib through the streets. It is both a religious celebration and a proud expression of Sikh identity in British public life.

In Punjab, Vaisakhi also coincides with the spring harvest, making it a time of double celebration — the land’s abundance reflecting God’s provision. British Sikhs with family in Punjab often feel a strong cultural connection to the harvest dimension of the festival.

Key Fact

Vaisakhi 1699 was the most significant day in the history of the Sikh community after Guru Nanak’s founding revelation — Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa, created the Panj Pyare, and established the tradition of Amrit Sanskar initiation. In Britain, the nagar kirtan procession on Vaisakhi is one of the largest Sikh public celebrations in Europe.

Divali: Bandi Chhor Divas

Sikhs celebrate Divali but for a specifically Sikh reason: it is called Bandi Chhor Divas — “the day of liberation.” The sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, was imprisoned in Gwalior Fort by the Mughal Emperor Jahangir. When the Emperor finally agreed to release him, Guru Hargobind refused to leave unless 52 Hindu princes who were also imprisoned were freed at the same time. The Emperor agreed, and Guru Hargobind returned to Amritsar to cheering crowds holding lights — hence the festival of lights.

The story of Bandi Chhor Divas is characteristic of Sikh values: standing for the freedom of others, not just one’s own. Guru Hargobind’s refusal to be freed without the other prisoners reflects the Sikh commitment to justice and equality. It is also significant that the Golden Temple at Amritsar was illuminated to welcome Guru Hargobind back, establishing a tradition of lighting the gurdwara at Divali that continues to this day.

Sikhs and Hindus both celebrate Divali but for different reasons. For many Hindus, Divali marks the return of Lord Rama from exile and the victory of good over evil. For Sikhs, Divali is Bandi Chhor Divas — the release of Guru Hargobind and the 52 princes. This is an important distinction to make in exam answers. The two traditions share the outward customs of lights and fireworks but the religious meanings are distinct. Students should not assume that because Sikhs celebrate Divali they are celebrating the same event as Hindus — Sikhism is a distinct religion with its own historical memory.

A common misconception is to conflate the Naam Karan ceremony with Amrit Sanskar (the Khalsa initiation ceremony). They are distinct. Naam Karan is performed shortly after birth: the baby is brought to the gurdwara, the Guru Granth Sahib is opened at random, and the first letter of the left-hand page determines the child’s name. No vows are taken and no commitment to the Khalsa is made — the ceremony is an act of thanksgiving and of placing the child under the guidance of the Guru’s word from the very beginning of life. Amrit Sanskar, by contrast, is a fully voluntary initiation taken in adulthood (or late adolescence), in which a person chooses to become an amritdhari Sikh and accepts the discipline of the Khalsa Rehat Maryada (code of conduct). A Sikh who has been through Naam Karan has not thereby become an amritdhari — full initiation requires a separate, conscious commitment. Examiners reward this distinction.

Gurpurbs

Gurpurbs are festivals marking anniversaries associated with the Sikh Gurus. The most widely celebrated is Guru Nanak’s birthday (Guru Nanak Gurpurb), usually in November. It is celebrated with an akhand path, kirtan, langar and nagar kirtan. Other major Gurpurbs include the birthday of Guru Gobind Singh and the martyrdom anniversaries of Guru Arjan Dev and Guru Tegh Bahadur (who were executed for refusing to convert to Islam — martyred for the right of religious freedom).

In India, Gurpurbs are celebrated with massive processions, especially in Punjab and at Nanded (where Guru Gobind Singh died). In Britain, Gurpurbs are celebrated in ways that reflect the British context: nagar kirtan through city streets, open days at gurdwaras welcoming non-Sikh visitors, and community events. The way Gurpurbs are celebrated in Britain reflects the diasporic Sikh community’s dual identity — rooted in Punjabi heritage and simultaneously British citizens making their traditions visible in British public life.

Birth and Naming Ceremonies

When a Sikh child is born, thanksgiving to God is expressed at the gurdwara as soon as the mother is well enough. An akhand path may be performed to mark the birth. The formal naming ceremony is called Naam Karan. The family brings the baby to the gurdwara, where the ardas (Sikh prayer of supplication) is offered. The Guru Granth Sahib is then opened at a random page and the first letter of the first hymn on the left-hand page is read aloud by the granthi. The family chooses a name beginning with that letter. This practice expresses the belief that the child’s identity is shaped from the first moment by the Guru’s word.

After the name is announced, the congregation calls out Waheguru Ji Ka Khalsa, Waheguru Ji Ki Fateh (“The Khalsa belongs to the Wondrous Lord; victory belongs to the Wondrous Lord”) as a communal blessing. Karah prashad (a sweet sanctified food made from equal measures of flour, butter and sugar) is distributed to the congregation — the equal portions expressing the equality of all present.

Historic Gurdwaras: The Golden Temple

The Golden Temple (Harimandir Sahib — “Temple of God”) at Amritsar in Punjab is the most sacred site in Sikhism. It was built under the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan Dev, and completed in 1604. Unlike Hindu temples, the Golden Temple was built with four doors, one on each side, signifying that it is open to people from all four directions — a physical expression of the Sikh teaching that all are welcome regardless of caste, religion or background.

The Golden Temple sits in the middle of a sacred pool of water (Amrit Sarovar — the “pool of nectar,” which gives Amritsar its name). Visiting the Golden Temple is considered an act of great devotion. Many British Sikhs make a pilgrimage to Amritsar at some point in their lives, especially at Vaisakhi. Unusually for the Sikh tradition — which does not have an obligatory pilgrimage — visiting the Golden Temple carries deep emotional and spiritual significance for Sikhs worldwide.

Key Fact

The Golden Temple (Harimandir Sahib) at Amritsar was built with four doors — one on each side — to signal that it is open to all people from every direction and every background. This architectural feature is a physical expression of the Sikh belief in the equality of all humanity before God.

3c28f2ae-af65-407c-9921-efccf86de663.title: Punishment: Aims, Types & the Death Penalty
3c28f2ae-af65-407c-9921-efccf86de663.content_html:
The Aims of Punishment

When someone breaks the law, society must decide how to respond. Punishment serves several purposes, and religious believers often disagree about which aim should be prioritised. The three main aims studied in GCSE Religious Studies are retribution, deterrence and reformation.

Retribution means making the criminal “pay” for what they have done. It is based on the idea that wrongdoing deserves a proportionate response. The Old Testament teaches “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exodus 21:24), suggesting that punishment should match the severity of the crime. In Islam, the Qur’an also permits retribution: “We ordained for them: a life for a life, an eye for an eye” (5:45).

Deterrence aims to discourage crime by showing the consequences of breaking the law. If people see that criminals are punished severely, they may be less likely to commit crimes themselves. Both Christianity and Islam support the idea that clear consequences help maintain social order, though they disagree about how harsh those consequences should be.

Key Fact

Reformation focuses on helping criminals change their behaviour and become productive members of society. Many Christians prioritise reformation, following Jesus’s teaching about forgiveness and second chances. The Parable of the Lost Son (Luke 15:11–32) shows God welcoming back those who have strayed, suggesting that criminals can be redeemed. Islam also supports reformation — the Qur’an teaches: “But whoever repents after his wrongdoing and reforms, indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness” (5:39).

The Treatment of Criminals

There are several ways in which criminals can be punished. Each method serves different aims and raises different ethical questions.

Prison removes criminals from society to protect the public, and provides time for reformation through education and rehabilitation programmes. However, critics argue that prisons can be “universities of crime,” where offenders learn new criminal skills. Many religious organisations, including Prison Fellowship (a Christian charity), work within prisons to support rehabilitation and spiritual growth.

Corporal punishment means inflicting physical pain on the body — such as caning, flogging or beating. It is banned in the UK but remains legal in some countries. Some Muslims argue that corporal punishment is supported by the Qur’an for certain offences, but others argue that it is outdated and contradicts the principle of mercy. Most Christians oppose corporal punishment, arguing that Jesus taught forgiveness rather than physical retribution.

Community service requires offenders to do unpaid work that benefits the local community. It can serve both deterrence (the offender must give up their time) and reformation (the work may help them develop skills and a sense of responsibility). Many religious believers support community service as a humane alternative to prison, particularly for less serious offences.

The Death Penalty

The death penalty (capital punishment) is the most extreme form of punishment — the state-sanctioned execution of a person convicted of a serious crime. It was abolished in the UK in 1965 but remains legal in many countries, including parts of the USA, China, Iran and Saudi Arabia.

Key Fact

Two key ethical principles apply to the death penalty debate. The principle of utility (utilitarianism) argues that the morality of an action depends on its consequences — if the death penalty deters crime and protects society, it produces the greatest good for the greatest number. The sanctity of life principle argues that all human life is sacred and belongs to God, so no human being has the right to take another’s life, regardless of what they have done.

Arguments for: It acts as the ultimate deterrent — people may be less likely to commit serious crimes if they know they could be executed. It provides retribution — some argue that the most serious crimes (such as serial murder or terrorism) deserve the ultimate punishment. It permanently protects society from the most dangerous criminals. The principle of utility may support it if it saves more lives than it takes.

Arguments against: It violates the sanctity of life — only God has the right to take life. Innocent people may be wrongly convicted and executed, and this cannot be undone. It does not allow for reformation — the criminal can never change or make amends. It reduces the state to the level of the murderer. Evidence suggests that the death penalty does not actually deter crime more effectively than long prison sentences.

Contrasting Beliefs on the Death Penalty and Corporal Punishment

Christianity: Most modern Christian denominations oppose the death penalty. Pope Francis declared in 2018 that the death penalty is “inadmissible” and called for its worldwide abolition. The Church of England also opposes it. Christians argue that Jesus taught forgiveness (“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” — Luke 23:34) and that the death penalty denies the possibility of reformation. However, some Christians point to the Old Testament, which prescribed death for certain offences, as evidence that God sometimes sanctions extreme punishment.

Islam: Islamic law (Shari’ah) permits the death penalty for certain serious offences, including murder and apostasy. However, the Qur’an also encourages mercy: “But whoever forgoes it as charity, it is an expiation for him” (5:45), suggesting that forgiveness is preferred. In practice, many Muslim scholars argue that the conditions for applying the death penalty under Shari’ah are extremely strict and rarely met. Regarding corporal punishment, some forms are prescribed in Islamic law (such as flogging for certain offences), but many modern Muslim scholars argue these should be understood in their historical context.

Key similarity: Both religions teach the sanctity of life and emphasise that mercy and forgiveness are virtues. Both encourage reformation of criminals where possible.

Key difference: Most mainstream Christian denominations now firmly oppose the death penalty, seeing it as incompatible with Jesus’s teachings on forgiveness. Islamic law technically permits it for certain offences, though many Muslim scholars argue that mercy should prevail and that the conditions for its application are extremely difficult to meet in practice.

3f8e7f3a-b0a1-49e1-8e6a-aa6227e93eee.title: Abortion & Euthanasia
3f8e7f3a-b0a1-49e1-8e6a-aa6227e93eee.content_html:
Sanctity of Life & Quality of Life

Two key concepts underpin religious and ethical debates about abortion and euthanasia. The sanctity of life is the belief that all human life is sacred because it is created by God. Christians point to Genesis 1:27: “God created mankind in his own image.” Muslims believe Allah breathes a soul into every person: “It is He who created you from clay, then determined a term for you” (Qur’an 6:2).

The quality of life is a different concept — it considers whether a person’s life is worth living based on their level of comfort, independence, happiness and freedom from pain. Some people argue that when quality of life is extremely poor, ending suffering may be the most compassionate response.

Key Fact

The tension between sanctity of life and quality of life is at the heart of both the abortion and euthanasia debates. Those who prioritise sanctity argue that life must never be deliberately ended. Those who emphasise quality of life argue that sometimes ending suffering is the most loving and compassionate thing to do.

Abortion

Abortion is the deliberate termination of a pregnancy. In England, Scotland and Wales, abortion is legal up to 24 weeks under the Abortion Act 1967 (amended 1990), provided two doctors agree that continuing the pregnancy poses a risk to the physical or mental health of the mother or existing children. After 24 weeks, abortion is only permitted if the mother’s life is at risk or the foetus has a severe abnormality.

Catholic Church: Abortion is always wrong because life begins at conception and is sacred. The Catechism states: “Human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception.” The only exception is if a medical procedure to save the mother’s life indirectly causes the death of the foetus (the principle of double effect).

Church of England: Abortion is generally opposed but accepted in certain circumstances, such as when the mother’s life is at risk, in cases of severe foetal abnormality, or after rape. The decision should be made with compassion and careful thought.

Liberal Christians: Some argue that the most loving thing may be to allow abortion in difficult circumstances. They apply Jesus’s teaching of compassion and the principle of “the lesser of two evils.”

Most Muslim scholars oppose abortion after ensoulment (when the soul enters the body), traditionally believed to occur at 120 days. Before this point, some scholars permit abortion in certain circumstances, such as when the mother’s life is in danger. The Qur’an (17:31) warns: “Do not kill your children for fear of poverty.”

If the mother’s life is at risk, most scholars agree that her life takes priority because she has existing responsibilities and relationships. However, abortion for convenience or non-medical reasons is generally considered haram.

Euthanasia

Euthanasia means deliberately ending someone’s life to relieve suffering. It is sometimes called “mercy killing.” There are different types: voluntary euthanasia (the person requests it), non-voluntary euthanasia (the person cannot give consent, e.g. in a coma), and assisted suicide (helping someone end their own life). All forms of euthanasia and assisted suicide are illegal in the UK.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam oppose euthanasia. Christians believe life is a gift from God and only God should decide when it ends. Job 1:21 says: “The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away.” Islam teaches that only Allah determines the time of death: “No soul can die except by Allah’s leave” (Qur’an 3:145). However, both religions support palliative care to relieve suffering without hastening death.

Arguments for: People should have the right to choose how and when they die. Forcing someone to live in extreme pain is cruel. Quality of life matters — when there is no hope of recovery, euthanasia may be the most compassionate option. Some argue Jesus’s Golden Rule (“Do to others what you would have them do to you” — Matthew 7:12) supports ending suffering.

Arguments against: Life is sacred and belongs to God — humans do not have the right to end it. Euthanasia could lead to a “slippery slope” where vulnerable people feel pressured to die. Modern palliative care can manage pain effectively. The Qur’an teaches patience in suffering: “Allah does not burden a soul beyond that it can bear” (2:286).

Death & the Afterlife

Religious beliefs about what happens after death influence attitudes towards euthanasia and the value of life.

Christianity: Most Christians believe in an afterlife. The soul continues after death — the righteous go to heaven (eternal life with God) and the unrighteous face judgement. Jesus said: “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die” (John 11:25). This belief gives Christians hope and comfort in the face of death.

Islam: Muslims believe in Yawm al-Din (the Day of Judgement), when Allah will resurrect all people and judge their deeds. The righteous will enter Jannah (paradise) and the wicked will be sent to Jahannam (hell). This belief means Muslims see life as a test and believe suffering has a purpose — it builds patience and strengthens faith.

Belief in an afterlife reinforces opposition to euthanasia. If this life is a preparation for eternal life, then cutting it short may have spiritual consequences. Christians may fear that taking one’s own life or assisting death goes against God’s plan. Muslims believe that accepting suffering patiently is rewarded in the afterlife. However, some non-religious people argue that without an afterlife, reducing suffering in this life becomes even more important — supporting the case for euthanasia.

Key Fact

Humanists and atheists, who do not believe in an afterlife, argue that moral decisions should focus on reducing suffering in this life. They may support euthanasia because they believe people have the right to die with dignity. This contrasts with religious views that see suffering as meaningful and life as belonging to God.

4ddc74fe-f047-4d1b-a7b4-af8694e05ba6.title: The Environment & Animal Rights
4ddc74fe-f047-4d1b-a7b4-af8694e05ba6.content_html:
Use & Abuse of the Environment

The environment faces serious threats from human activity. Pollution of air, water and land damages ecosystems and harms human health. Climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, threatens the future of the planet. Religious believers see protecting the environment as a moral duty.

The use of natural resources such as oil, gas, coal, water and timber is essential for modern life. However, many of these resources are finite — they will eventually run out. Religious teachings call on humans to use resources responsibly, not wastefully.

Key Fact

Christians believe in stewardship — caring for creation on God’s behalf. Genesis 2:15 says God placed humans in the Garden of Eden “to work it and take care of it.” Pope Francis’s encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015) described the earth as “our common home” and called for urgent action on climate change and pollution.

Muslims believe humans are khalifah (caretakers) of the earth. The Qur’an (6:165) says: “It is He who has made you successors upon the earth.” Wasting resources is considered wrong. The Prophet Muhammad taught: “Do not waste water even if you are at a running stream.” Muslims believe they will be accountable to Allah on the Day of Judgement for how they treated the environment.

Many religious organisations actively campaign for environmental protection. Christian organisations like A Rocha work on conservation projects worldwide. The Church of England has committed to achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2030. Islamic Relief has environmental programmes addressing deforestation and water pollution. The Islamic Declaration on Global Climate Change (2015) urged Muslims to take action based on their role as khalifah. These responses show that religious environmental teaching is not just theoretical — it drives real-world action.

Use & Abuse of Animals

Humans use animals in many ways: for food, clothing, medical research, entertainment and companionship. Religious traditions have varying views on how animals should be treated and whether these uses are morally acceptable.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam teach that animals are part of God’s creation and should be treated with respect. However, most religious traditions accept that humans have a higher status than animals. Genesis 1:28 gives humans dominion (authority) over animals. The Qur’an says Allah “subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and on the earth” (45:13).

Animal Experimentation

Animal experimentation involves testing medicines, treatments or products on animals. This is one of the AQA “contrasting beliefs” topics — you must be able to explain different religious views.

In favour: Many Christians accept animal experimentation if it is necessary to save human lives or reduce suffering. Humans have dominion over animals (Genesis 1:28) and are uniquely made in God’s image. The Catholic Church teaches that animal experimentation is morally acceptable “if it remains within reasonable limits and contributes to caring for or saving human lives.”

Against: Some Christians, particularly Quakers, oppose animal experimentation because it causes unnecessary suffering. They argue that stewardship means protecting all of God’s creatures. Proverbs 12:10 says: “The righteous care for the needs of their animals.” The RSPCA was founded by an Anglican clergyman, reflecting Christian concern for animal welfare.

In favour (with conditions): Some Muslim scholars permit animal experimentation if it is genuinely necessary for medical advances and there is no alternative. Saving human life is a high priority in Islam: “Whoever saves a life, it is as if he has saved all of humanity” (Qur’an 5:32).

Against: Islam generally opposes unnecessary harm to animals. The Prophet Muhammad said: “If anyone wrongfully kills even a sparrow, he will have to answer for it on the Day of Judgement.” Animals are part of Allah’s creation and deserve compassion. Causing pain for cosmetic testing or trivial purposes is considered haram (forbidden).

The Use of Animals for Food

Both Christianity and Islam allow eating meat, but both have rules about how animals should be treated. Christians have no specific dietary laws (Jesus declared all foods clean in Mark 7:19), though many Christians choose to eat less meat or become vegetarian out of concern for animal welfare and the environment.

Islam requires that meat be halal (permissible). Animals must be slaughtered humanely in the name of Allah, with a sharp knife to minimise suffering. Pork is haram. The Qur’an (5:3) lists forbidden foods. These rules reflect Islam’s teaching that animals should be treated with respect even when used for food.

Key Fact

Non-religious perspectives on animal rights are also important. The philosopher Peter Singer argues that animals have the capacity to suffer and therefore deserve moral consideration. Vegetarians and vegans often argue that it is wrong to use animals for food when plant-based alternatives exist. Animal rights organisations like the RSPCA campaign against factory farming and animal cruelty.

5147a507-986d-46ad-ad77-89bf27b44533.title: The Gurdwara: Worship and Community
5147a507-986d-46ad-ad77-89bf27b44533.content_html:
What is a Gurdwara?

The word gurdwara means “doorway to the Guru” (from Punjabi: gur = Guru, dwara = door or gateway). Every gurdwara is defined by the presence of the Guru Granth Sahib — the eternal, living scripture that Sikhs regard as their eleventh and final Guru. Without the Guru Granth Sahib, a building is not a gurdwara. This understanding shapes everything about how the gurdwara is designed and used.

There are over 250 registered gurdwaras in the United Kingdom, serving the approximately 430,000 Sikhs in Britain. The largest is the Gurdwara Sri Guru Singh Sabha in Southall, west London — the largest gurdwara outside India — which can accommodate over 3,000 worshippers and serves langar to thousands of people each week. Gurdwaras in cities including Birmingham, Leicester, Bradford and Glasgow are centres of spiritual, cultural and social life for their local Sikh communities.

Design and Features

From the outside, a gurdwara is identifiable by the Nishan Sahib — a tall flagpole flying a triangular dark blue flag bearing the Khanda (the Sikh emblem). Inside, the main prayer hall is called the Darbar Sahib (literally “court of the Lord”). Worshippers remove their shoes and cover their heads before entering as a mark of respect. They then bow before the Guru Granth Sahib and make an offering.

The prayer hall has no fixed seating or pews. The congregation sits on the floor — regardless of age, gender or status — which itself expresses the Sikh belief in equality. There is no distinction between where men and women sit in the prayer hall of a gurdwara; they may sit on either side or intermixed, depending on local practice, but the principle is complete equality.

Key Fact

The two most important features in the gurdwara prayer hall are the palki (throne-canopy) and the takht (throne or royal seat). Together they represent the sovereignty and living authority of the Guru Granth Sahib.

The Palki and the Takht

The palki is the ornate canopy or palanquin structure under which the Guru Granth Sahib rests. It is typically elaborately decorated and elevated, signalling the supreme honour in which the scripture is held. The palki symbolises the royal status of the Guru Granth Sahib — just as an earthly king might sit under a canopy, the eternal Guru sits under its palki.

The takht (throne) is the raised platform or seat on which the Guru Granth Sahib is placed. The word takht literally means “throne.” Together, the palki (canopy) and the takht (throne) communicate that the Guru Granth Sahib is not just a book — it is the living, reigning Guru of the Sikh community, deserving of the same honour as a Guru in human form. Beside the takht stands the chauri — a fan waved over the Guru Granth Sahib as a mark of honour, similar to the fans once used to cool royalty.

The Guru Granth Sahib is treated with the same care as a living person. At the end of each day in many gurdwaras, the scripture is ceremonially “put to rest” in a dedicated room called the sukhasan room, wrapped in cloth (rumala). In the morning, it is ceremonially brought back to the prayer hall in a procession. This practice underlines the Sikh belief that the Guru Granth Sahib is not a sacred object but a living presence — the Guru who is always available to the community.

The Gurdwara’s Role in the Community

The gurdwara is far more than a place of formal worship. It is the social, cultural and spiritual heart of the Sikh community. The original vision of Guru Nanak was that the gurdwara should serve three interconnected purposes, sometimes described as the three pillars of Sikhism: Naam Japna (meditation on God’s name), Kirat Karni (honest work) and Vand Chakna (sharing with others). All three are expressed in and through the gurdwara.

The gurdwara hosts the langar (free communal kitchen), classes in Punjabi, Sikh history and scripture, ceremonies for birth, naming, marriage and death, and welfare services for those in need. In many British cities, gurdwaras have opened food banks, offered shelter to homeless people, and provided community support during times of national crisis — including during the COVID-19 pandemic. This is sewa in action.

Sikh practice is not confined to the gurdwara. The Guru Granth Sahib at GGS 305:4 emphasises the importance of prayer and remembrance of God in the home. Amritdhari Sikhs observe the Nitnem — a set of daily prayers including Japji Sahib (composed by Guru Nanak) in the morning, and further prayers in the evening and at night. Many Sikh families maintain a dedicated space in the home for the Guru Granth Sahib or for a prayer area. The home is understood as an extension of the gurdwara in spiritual terms — the family that prays together strengthens the sangat in miniature.

Sahajdhari Sikhs — those who follow Sikh teachings but have not undergone formal initiation — may practise Nitnem and maintain home prayer spaces without being bound by all the obligations of the Khalsa. The principle of prayer in the home (GGS 305:4) applies to all Sikhs, amritdhari and sahajdhari alike.

Key Fact

The gurdwara serves the whole community, not just practising Sikhs. It hosts the langar (free communal meal), welfare services, education and ceremonies — expressing the Sikh teaching that sewa (service) is not optional but a dimension of worship. In Britain, gurdwaras have been at the forefront of community support in times of hardship.
